docs.title: Parakeet
docs.text:
A data-parallel compiler for numerical Python.

Write ordinary NumPy, Python loops, comprehensions, or explicit data-parallel operators (par.map, par.reduce, par.fold, par.scan, par.allpairs). Parakeet specializes your function for its input types, fuses and tiles the array math, and compiles native code for multi-core CPUs, Apple Metal, and NVIDIA CUDA.

Get started Explore the gallery

docs.title: Exact nearest neighbor
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import parakeet as par


@par.jit
def nearest(x, y):
  delta = x[:, None, :] - y[None, :, :]
  d2 = np.sum(delta ** np.float32(2), axis=2)
  return np.argmin(d2, axis=1)

Parakeet streams distances a tile at a time on both CPU and GPU, keeping only the winning index per tile rather than allocating the N × M distance matrix. Ties preserve NumPy's exact first-index rule.

Compare timings, scaling, and memory

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
python -m pip install parakeet

Requires Python 3.11+, NumPy 2, and a system C compiler. For GPU backends, install parakeet[metal] on Apple Silicon or parakeet[cuda12] with an NVIDIA GPU.

docs.title: What Parakeet gives you
docs.text:
Idiomatic Python & NumPy

Write NumPy expressions, comprehensions, explicit loops, @dataclass modules, or explicit operators (par.map, par.fold, par.scan, par.scatter_add, par.wavefront). Unsupported constructs fail loudly with your exact source line.

Compiled language · Operators

Automatic Fusion & Tiling

Chained array expressions, boolean filters, same-key histograms, matrix products, pairwise distances, and online softmax attention fuse and tile into cache or GPU shared memory without materializing giant intermediates.

How Parakeet optimizes · Algebraic laws

Composable Gradients

par.grad, par.value_and_grad, par.jvp, par.vjp, and par.hvp differentiate directly through loops, arrays, and @dataclass parameters—so forward pass, backward pass, and optimizer compile into one native step.

Automatic differentiation

Multi-core CPU, Metal & CUDA

One Python function compiles to sequential C, multi-core threads, OpenMP, GCD, Apple Metal, or NVIDIA CUDA (with TF32 Tensor Cores). Keep arrays resident on device across calls with par.to_device.

Backends and GPUs · Benchmarks

docs.title: NumPy, comprehensions, operators, or loops
docs.text:
Write whichever style fits your algorithm. The first three functions below compile to the same single-pass parallel loop with no temporary arrays; the explicit for loop compiles to a single sequential C loop:

@par.jit
def via_numpy(x, alpha=0.5, beta=0.3):
  return np.tanh(x * alpha) + beta


@par.jit
def via_comprehension(x, alpha=0.5, beta=0.3):
  return np.array([np.tanh(xi * alpha) + beta for xi in x])


@par.jit
def via_operator(x, alpha=0.5, beta=0.3):
  return par.map(lambda xi: np.tanh(xi * alpha) + beta, x)


@par.jit
def via_loop(x, alpha=0.5, beta=0.3):
  y = np.empty_like(x, dtype=float)
  for i in range(len(x)):
    y[i] = np.tanh(x[i] * alpha) + beta
  return y

docs.title: Algebraic laws
docs.text:
Simple loop fusion eliminates element-wise temporaries, but harder bottlenecks remain whenever a program normalizes across a whole row (O(N²) attention or O(M · V) cross-entropy), chains matrix contractions, runs a long serial recurrence (O(T) depth), or saves a giant tape for reverse-mode AD.

Instead of hardcoding model-specific "fused layers", Parakeet encodes these optimizations as six general algebraic laws over its index-space primitives. Because the passes match operator algebra rather than neural-network layer names, the exact same passes optimize Gaussian kernel regression, exact 1-NN, GBDT histograms, and IIR filters alongside attention, cross-entropy, and state-space models.

docs.title: Semantic contract: real algebra vs. exact order
docs.text:
• Associative / commutative rewrites (parallel reductions, monoidal tiling, contraction reassociation, chunkwise scans, privatized scatter-add) assume real-arithmetic associativity: floating-point rounding may differ in the last ULP relative to a left-to-right loop, just like NumPy's pairwise summation or cuBLAS.
  • Order-sensitive operations (first-index ties and NaNs in argmin/argmax, non-commutative par.fold merges, arbitrary user folds) preserve exact left-to-right merge order.

docs.title: The six laws at a glance
docs.text: Law Core idea Compiler pass Workloads 1. Rescaled semiring monoids Associative rescaling state (m, l, o) monoidal tiling Softmax attention, Split-K decode, linear cross-entropy, RBF regression, 1-pass logsumexp 2. Algebraic AD rematerialization Recompute score tiles from sufficient statistics algebraic_vjp Attention backward, cross-entropy backward, 1-pass LayerNorm / RMSNorm VJP 3. Bilinear contraction reassociation Reorder (U @ Vᵀ) @ Wᵀ + share KV head tiles contraction reassociation Multi-head latent attention (MLA), grouped-query attention (GQA), low-rank chains 4. Chunkwise state-space duality Block-parallel affine / bilinear composition chunkwise scan Parallel IIR / EMA / Kalman filters, Mamba-2 & gated linear attention 5. Affine tile-interval pruning Propagate [i₀, i₀+Bₘ-1] × [j₀, j₀+Bₙ-1] bounds TileInterval Causal & sliding-window masks, banded matrices, spatial cutoffs 6. Privatized scatter & ordered carries Thread-private histograms & tiled ordered folds IndexScatter, pairwise fold tiling GBDT tree splits, exact 1-NN, multi-channel BAM pileup, par.fold

docs.title: Law 1: Rescaled semiring monoids
docs.text:
The problem. Softmax attention, linear cross-entropy, and Gaussian kernel regression all normalize by a row-wide max and sum(exp(...)) before taking a weighted sum—naively requiring O(N · M) or O(M · V) buffers.

The law. Maintaining the running maximum m, normalizing sum l, and unnormalized output o forms an associative monoid (S, ⊕, e):

m = max(m₁, m₂) (m₁, l₁, o₁) ⊕ (m₂, l₂, o₂) = (   m,   l₁ · exp(m₁ − m) + l₂ · exp(m₂ − m),   o₁ · exp(m₁ − m) + o₂ · exp(m₂ − m) )

Because ⊕ is associative, tiles can be reduced in cache or GPU shared memory and merged in any grouping without materializing the full score matrix:

Where it fires:

  • Tiled softmax attention (flash_monoid): streams K, V tiles against Q with zero S/P allocation.
  • Split-K decoding (split_k=True): when query count is tiny (decode) and T_kv is long, splits T_kv across GPU threadblocks and merges partial (mₚ, lₚ, oₚ) summaries with ⊕.
  • Tiled linear cross-entropy (monoid_lse): tiles H @ W over vocabulary V with the scalar (m, l) monoid, eliminating the M × V logit tensor.
  • Gaussian / RBF kernel regression (score_op="sqdist"): fuses -γ · ‖xᵢ − yⱼ‖² into the same O(N + M) streaming kernel.

docs.title: Law 2: Algebraic rematerialization in reverse-mode AD
docs.text:
The problem. A naive reverse-mode tape saves every forward intermediate, bringing back O(T²) memory for attention and O(M · V) memory for linear cross-entropy.

The law. Before loop lowering, parakeet/transforms/algebraic_vjp.py substitutes sufficient-statistic adjoints that save only compact O(T · D) tensors and recompute score tiles on-chip during backpropagation:

Where it fires:

  • Attention backward (flash_monoid_bwd): saves (Q, K, V, O, lse), computes Dᵢ = ∑_d dO[i, d] · O[i, d], and recomputes P = exp(S − lse) and dS = P · (dO @ Vᵀ − D) tile-by-tile (also composes with forward-over-reverse par.hvp).
  • Linear cross-entropy backward (cce_bwd): saves (H, W, targets, lse) and recomputes p[i, v] = exp(hᵢ · wᵥ − lseᵢ) on-chip.
  • LayerNorm / RMSNorm & softmax VJPs: collapses multi-pass backward graphs into one pass (dS = P · (dP − ∑ P · dP), dropping the max adjoint).

docs.title: Law 3: Bilinear contraction reassociation & shared-KV tiling
docs.text:
The problem. Chaining two bilinear contractions ((X @ A) @ B, or latent attention K = C_kv @ W_uk, V = C_kv @ W_uv, O = softmax(Q @ Kᵀ) @ V) can cost orders of magnitude more FLOPs and memory in the wrong parenthesization.

The law. For a single-use intermediate T = U @ Vᵀ feeding Y = W @ T:

(U · Vᵀ) · Wᵀ = U · (Vᵀ · Wᵀ)   — pick min( U·K·(R + P), P·R·(K + U) ) FLOPs Expanded (prefill optimal) materializes K, V 
K = C_kv @ W_uk
V = C_kv @ W_uv
O = softmax(Q @ K.T) @ V
Absorbed (decode optimal) stays in latent C_kv 
Q_abs = Q @ W_uk.T  # absorb W_uk into Q
O = (softmax(Q_abs @ C_kv.T) @ C_kv) @ W_uv

parakeet/transforms/reassociate.py emits a runtime shape-guarded branch so short-query decode runs tiled Law 1 attention directly over the compressed latent C_kv, while long-query prefill automatically takes the lower-FLOP expanded branch.

Shared-KV head-group tiling (GQA): when a head-group axis G of Q broadcasts against a single KV head, Parakeet folds G into the query row (i_eff = g * T_q + i) so all G query heads share one SRAM load of K and V.

docs.title: Law 4: Chunkwise state-space duality
docs.text:
The problem. Plain Python recurrences (for t in range(T): s = a[t] * s + b[t]) have O(T) serial depth and leave multi-core CPUs and GPUs idle.

The law. Affine maps compose associatively, (a₂, b₂) ∘ (a₁, b₁) = (a₂ · a₁, a₂ · b₁ + b₂). parakeet/transforms/tile_scan.py partitions time into chunks of C = 64 and rewrites both scalar affine loops (EMA, IIR, Kalman) and bilinear matrix-state loops (Mamba-2 / gated linear attention) into a division-free parallel scan:

What you write O(T) serial depth 
for t in range(T):
  S = a[t] * S + k[t][:, None] * v[t][None, :]
  out[t] = q[t] @ S
Compiled schedule (C = 64) 64× shorter scan + GEMMs 
L, A = chunk_decay_products(a, C=64)  # parallel, zero-safe
Y_intra = ((Q_c @ K_c.T) * L) @ V_c  # parallel over chunks
B_c = K_scaled.T @ V_c  # parallel chunk summaries
S_in = scan_affine(A, B_c)  # 64x shorter recurrence
out = Y_intra + (Q_c @ S_in)  # parallel readout

Because chunkwise scan runs before tiling, the matrix products in Steps 1, 2, and 4 flow directly into CPU register tiling, Metal simdgroup_matrix, and CUDA TF32 WMMA Tensor Cores.

docs.title: Law 5: Affine tile-interval mask pruning
docs.text:
The problem. Causal masks (j <= i), sliding windows (i - j <= W), and banded matrices evaluate millions of entries that are immediately discarded.

The law. TileInterval (parakeet/transforms/analysis.py) propagates coordinate intervals [i₀, i₀ + Bₘ − 1] × [j₀, j₀ + Bₙ − 1] through affine index predicates to classify every tile statically:

Tile condition Example (causal j <= i) Action emitted Always false j₀ > i₀ + Bₘ − 1 Skip tile before loading K or V Always true j₀ + Bₙ − 1 ≤ i₀ Branchless inner loop (mask check removed) Boundary / mixed i₀ − Bₙ < j₀ ≤ i₀ + Bₘ − 1 Evaluate per-element mask

Sliding-window masks ((j <= i) & (i - j <= W)) automatically drop from O(N²) to O(N · W) work. For runtime boolean mask arrays, GPU threadblocks cooperatively check whether any entry in the tile is true and skip empty tiles before loading values.

docs.title: Law 6: Privatized scatter & ordered multi-state carries
docs.text:
Two patterns dominate outside dense linear algebra: accumulating into shared bins (np.bincount, par.scatter_add) and folding structured state (argmin, Welford variance, par.fold).

  • Keyed histogram fusion: sibling IndexScatter statements sharing an index array (e.g. GBDT gradient/Hessian histograms or 6-channel BAM pileups) merge into one traversal, lowered with thread-private bins on CPU and parallel atomics on GPU.
  • Ordered pairwise tile folds: Fold.carries tracks multiple scalar fields in one pass while preserving chunk order. pairwise fold tiling fuses a pairwise score producer directly into an ordered fold over L1 / shared-memory tiles, eliminating O(Q · R) distance matrices in both broadcasting NumPy and nested-map 1-NN:

Next: Rewrite rules catalog lists every fusion, tiling, and differentiation rule and compares Parakeet 1.x with the 2013–2014 theses. See also the Kernel gallery for runnable examples across all six laws.

docs.title: parakeet.jit
docs.text:
Compile a numerical Python function to native code on first call.

Use it bare (@jit) or with options (@jit(backend="metal")). The function is specialised for each distinct combination of argument types; every later call with the same types runs the cached native code.

Options (all default to the corresponding parakeet.config setting):

backend "auto", "c", "multicore", "threads", "openmp", "gcd", "metal"/"mps", "cuda" or "python". bounds_check Raise IndexError for out-of-range indices instead of crashing. fusion Fuse array expressions into single loops. tiling Tile matmul-shaped loops for cache locality.

docs.title: parakeet.grad(f, argnum=0, *, wrt=None)
docs.text:
The gradient of the scalar-valued function f with respect to argnum / wrt.

argnum (or its keyword alias wrt) may be a positional index (0), a parameter name ("w"), or a tuple of indices/names ((0, 1), ("w", "b")). Works inside compiled code and from plain Python, including when calling the gradient function with keyword arguments.

docs.title: parakeet.value_and_grad(f, argnum=0, *, wrt=None)
docs.text: Like :func:grad, but the new function returns (f(*args), gradient).

docs.title: parakeet.jvp(fn, primals, tangents)
docs.text:
Forward-mode Jacobian-vector product: returns (fn(*primals), d_fn).

primals and tangents are tuples of arguments matching fn (or single values for unary functions). Works from plain Python and inside @par.jit or other AD transforms with zero tape and O(1) extra memory.

docs.title: parakeet.vjp(fn, *primals)
docs.text:
General non-scalar reverse-mode AD: returns (primal_out, vjp_fn).

vjp_fn(cotangent) returns a tuple of input cotangents matching primals for arbitrary scalar, array, tuple, record, or RaggedArray outputs.

docs.title: parakeet.linearize(fn, *primals)
docs.text: Linearize fn at primals: returns (primal_out, lin_fn) where lin_fn(*tangents) computes the directional derivative JVP(fn, primals, tangents).

docs.title: parakeet.linear_transpose(linear_fn, *example_inputs)
docs.text: Return transpose_fn(cotangent) computing L^T(cotangent) for a linear function L.

docs.text:

Runs in ~2x reverse-mode cost with zero O(N^2) Hessian allocation.

docs.title: parakeet.DeviceArray
docs.text:
An array resident on a GPU device (Metal or CUDA) across @jit calls.

Created with :func:parakeet.to_device or returned automatically by a @jit function called with DeviceArray inputs. Passing a DeviceArray into subsequent @jit calls on the same device avoids redundant host-to-device uploads, and GPU-computed outputs are promoted directly to DeviceArray without device-to-host downloads — keeping weights, gradients, and optimizer state resident on the GPU throughout a training loop.

Call :meth:numpy or :func:parakeet.to_host (or np.asarray(da)) to bring the contents back to host memory.

docs.title: parakeet.fold(el, lift, merge, x, init=None, *, axis=None, indexed=False, emit=None)
docs.text:
Lift elements to scalar/fixed-vector tuple states and merge adjacent states in input order.

With no axis, lift each leading slice and return one state. With an axis, fold the lanes along that axis and project each state with emit (which may return a scalar, a fixed-size array, or a tuple/NamedTuple of them). An indexed lift receives (value, index) with the index local to its lane. A supplied seed is applied once on the left; an unseeded empty fold raises.

docs.title: parakeet.errors
docs.text:
Exception hierarchy.

Compile-time problems are reported as :class:CompileError subclasses that carry the location of the offending Python source, so the message points at the user's code rather than at Parakeet internals. Runtime problems detected by generated code (out-of-bounds indices, shape mismatches, ...) are re-raised as the same built-in exception NumPy/Python would have raised.

docs.title: Automatic differentiation
docs.text: Parakeet differentiates functions directly at the operator level, so derivatives go through the same fusion, cache/GPU tiling, and parallel code generation as the forward pass.

docs.title: Forward mode vs. reverse mode
docs.text:
For a function f: Rⁿ → Rᵐ with Jacobian J (shape m × n), choose the mode that matches your input/output shape:

  • Reverse mode (par.grad, par.vjp, par.jacrev) computes a vector-Jacobian product uᵀ · J in cost proportional to outputs m. Use it when n ≫ m (scalar training losses, inverse problems).
  • Forward mode (par.jvp, par.jacfwd) computes a Jacobian-vector product J · v in cost proportional to inputs n with O(1) extra memory and no backward tape—even through long loops. Use it when m ≫ n, for directional derivatives, or inside forward-over-reverse par.hvp.

The two modes are exact linear transposes of one another for any input x, tangent v, and cotangent u:

⟨ jvp(f, x, v), u ⟩ = ⟨ v, vjp(f, x)(u) ⟩

docs.title: Reverse-mode gradients (grad and value_and_grad)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import parakeet as par


def loss(w, b, x, y):
  return np.mean((np.tanh(x @ w + b) - y) ** 2)


g = par.grad(loss)(w, b, x, y)  # d loss / d w
value, g = par.value_and_grad(loss, wrt="w")(w, b, x, y)  # by parameter name
gw, gb = par.grad(loss, wrt=("w", "b"))(x=x, y=y, w=w, b=b)  # keyword args work too

Differentiated arguments may be floats, float/complex arrays, RaggedArrays, or nested tuples, NamedTuples, fixed-key dicts, and @dataclass records (discrete fields like int, bool, or str pass through as zero-tangent leaves):

def mlp(params, x, y):
  (w1, b1), (w2, b2) = params
  h = np.tanh(x @ w1 + b1)
  return np.mean((h @ w2 + b2 - y) ** 2)


(gw1, gb1), (gw2, gb2) = par.grad(mlp)(params, x, y)

Calling par.grad inside @par.jit compiles the entire training loop into one native function (see Train nanoGPT and examples/convnet.py):

@par.jit
def descend(w, x, y, rate, steps):
  for _ in range(steps):
    w = w - rate * par.grad(loss)(w, x, y)
  return w

docs.title: Forward mode (jvp), general vjp, and higher-order AD
docs.text:
def f(x, w):
  z = np.tanh(x @ w)
  return z, np.sum(z * z, axis=1)


# Forward-mode JVP (O(1) extra memory, single forward pass)
(y1, y2), (dy1, dy2) = par.jvp(f, (x, w), (vx, vw))

# General non-scalar VJP
(y1, y2), pullback = par.vjp(f, x, w)
gx, gw = pullback((u1, u2))

par.hvp computes Hessian-vector products via forward-over-reverse (jvp(grad(f))) in one fused pass—including through checkpointed loops, LayerNorm, and tiled attention (recomputing score tiles on the fly without allocating T × T matrices):

def objective(w, x):
  h = np.tanh(x @ w)
  return np.sum(h * h * h)


hv = par.hvp(lambda w_: objective(w_, x), w, v)  # H(w) · v
H = par.hessian(lambda w_: objective(w_, x))(w)  # full Hessian
J_fwd = par.jacfwd(lambda w_: np.tanh(x @ w_))(w)
J_rev = par.jacrev(lambda w_: np.tanh(x @ w_))(w)

Nested reverse-over-reverse (par.grad(par.grad(...))) also works through element-wise ops, reductions, matmuls, views, stack/concatenate, cumsum, gather/scatter-add, and scalar par.map.

Loops not touching differentiated state are left untouched. Loops with break, continue, or early return over differentiated state—and runtime if branches containing array stores, return, break, or raise—fail loudly at compile time.

docs.title: Custom rules, stop_gradient, and checkpoint
docs.text:
• @par.jit(jvp=..., vjp=...) attaches custom rules with plain flat signatures:
  • jvp(*primals, *tangents) -> (output, d_output)
  • vjp(*primals) -> (output, pullback) where pullback(d_output) -> d_inputs (or pass a (fwd, bwd) tuple for explicit residuals)
def smooth_relu_jvp(x, dx):
  return np.maximum(x, 0.0), dx / (1.0 + np.exp(-x))


def smooth_relu_vjp(x):
  return np.maximum(x, 0.0), lambda dy: dy / (1.0 + np.exp(-x))


@par.jit(jvp=smooth_relu_jvp, vjp=smooth_relu_vjp)
def smooth_relu(x):
  return np.maximum(x, 0.0)
  • @par.jvp_for(fn) / @par.vjp_for(fn) register rules on an existing function (JAX-style @par.custom_jvp / @par.custom_vjp remain as aliases).
  • par.stop_gradient(x) detaches any scalar, array, record, or RaggedArray from both forward and reverse AD with zero copy.
  • @par.checkpoint discards forward intermediates for a block and rematerializes them during backprop, composing automatically with Law 2 algebraic rematerialization for attention, linear cross-entropy, softmax, and LayerNorm / RMSNorm.

docs.title: In-place stores and fail-loud guarantees
docs.text:
Slice assignments, indexed updates, and in-place additions (out[:3] = ..., out += bias, np.add.at) are differentiated accurately. Overwriting a buffer that an earlier backward rule still requires (y = np.tanh(h); h[0] = 5.0) is detected and refused at compile time.

Parakeet never silently drops gradients. Any unsupported operation on the differentiated path (such as np.cumprod, np.convolve, or arbitrary indexed overwrites out[idx] = v) raises an UnsupportedError naming the line:

UnsupportedError: cannot differentiate through cumprod() (line 12): its derivative is not implemented

Implementation modules: autodiff.py, jvp.py, algebraic_vjp.py.

docs.title: Multi-core CPU
docs.text:
• Outermost parallelism: map, allpairs, imap, parfor, array expressions, comprehensions, and associative reductions split across config.num_threads threads (default: all cores). Nested parallel ops run sequentially inside each worker.
  • Grain threshold: Cheap loops run on the calling thread unless they have at least 2 * config.parallel_grain iterations (default 8,192 per chunk). Loops containing inner loops always split.
  • Threads & processes: Compiled functions release the GIL and are safe to call concurrently from Python threads. With multiprocessing, use "threads" (fork-safe) or set start method "spawn" when using "openmp" or "gcd".

docs.title: Apple GPUs (Metal)
docs.text:
@par.jit(backend="metal")
def blur_energy(img):
  return (img[1:-1, 1:-1] * 4 - img[:-2, 1:-1] - img[2:, 1:-1] - img[1:-1, :-2] - img[1:-1, 2:]) ** 2

Eligible parallel loops compile to Metal Shading Language (MSL) compute kernels, using Apple Silicon's simdgroup_matrix FP32 hardware units automatically on tiled contractions.

Apple GPUs have no hardware float64

Loops touching float64 data fall back to the CPU thread pool with a FallbackWarning. Pass float32 arrays and np.float32 scalars to stay on Metal (Python float literals like x * 2.0 preserve float32 via NEP 50).

Loops also stay on CPU if they allocate dynamic arrays per iteration or call functions Metal lacks (lgamma, erfc). Control fallback behavior with config.device_fallback: "warn" (default), "silent", or "error". Runtime errors inside GPU kernels (IndexError, AssertionError) still raise normal Python exceptions.

docs.text:
@par.jit(backend="cuda")
def distances(X, C):
  return par.allpairs(lambda a, b: np.sum((a - b) ** 2), X, C)

Enable TF32 Tensor Cores (nvcuda::wmma) on sm_80+ GPUs with par.config.tensor_cores = True (or PARAKEET_TENSOR_CORES=1).

(TPUs are not supported: TPUs require XLA whole-program static-shape graphs, whereas Parakeet generates scalar C/MSL/CUDA kernels.)

CI simulator and GPU test validation

In CI (no NVIDIA hardware), PARAKEET_CUDA_SIMULATE=1 compiles generated CUDA kernels as host C++ and executes their thread grids on CPU.

Full physical-GPU runs (L4, A10, A100, T4) validate the test suite, examples, and benchmarks with strict device dispatch. To run tests on your own GPU:

docs.title: Device residency and data movement
docs.text:
Within a single @par.jit call, arrays stay on the GPU across consecutive kernels:

  1. The first GPU kernel touching an input uploads it; outputs allocated by the compiled function are created directly on the device (and on Apple Silicon unified memory, Metal shares buffers with zero copies).
  2. Later GPU kernels reuse resident buffers without copying back to the host.
  3. Temporary device buffers freed before the host touches them are never downloaded.
  4. Only host-side loops, CPU fallbacks, BLAS calls, or returning to Python pull modified buffers back to host memory.

Dispatch threshold: A parallel loop goes to the GPU when it has at least 1,024 elements and elements × estimated_inner_iters >= config.device_threshold (default 32,768). Tiny loops or low-parallelism outer loops stay on CPU where launch overhead would dominate.

Reusing inputs across calls: Wrap arrays with par.to_device to avoid re-uploading inputs on every call, and call par.to_host when Python needs the result:

x_dev = par.to_device(x, backend="cuda")
y_dev = my_kernel(x_dev)
y_np = par.to_host(y_dev)

docs.title: 1. FASTQ 2-bit canonical k-mers and read QC
docs.text:
Parakeet accepts list[str] directly (packing fixed-length strings into 2D uint8 or variable-length strings into RaggedArray[uint8]), compiles constant single-char dicts (BASE_CODE) into 256-byte LUTs, supports IntEnum alphabets, and unboxes multi-output par.map tuples into one parallel pass:

class Base(IntEnum):
  A = 0
  C = 1
  G = 2
  T = 3


BASE_CODE = {"A": Base.A, "C": Base.C, "G": Base.G, "T": Base.T}


@par.jit
def encode_canonical_kmers_and_gc(reads, quals, k):
  """Encode ASCII DNA reads (``list[str]`` or ``(N, L)`` uint8) into:
  - canonical 2-bit k-mers ``(N, L - k + 1)`` uint64  [min(fwd, revcomp)]
  - per-read GC fraction ``(N,)`` float32
  - per-read mean Phred quality ``(N,)`` float32
  """
  mask = (~np.uint64(0)) >> np.uint64(64 - 2 * k)
  rev_shift = np.uint64(2 * (k - 1))

  def encode_read(seq, qual):
    codes = BASE_CODE[seq]
    gc = np.mean((codes == Base.C) | (codes == Base.G)).astype(np.float32)
    mean_q = np.mean(qual.astype(np.float32) - 33.0)
    out = np.empty(len(seq) - k + 1, dtype=np.uint64)
    fwd = np.uint64(0)
    rev = np.uint64(0)
    for pos, c in enumerate(codes):
      code = np.uint64(c)
      fwd = ((fwd << np.uint64(2)) | code) & mask
      rev = (rev >> np.uint64(2)) | ((np.uint64(3) ^ code) << rev_shift)
      if pos >= k - 1:
        out[pos - k + 1] = min(fwd, rev)
    return out, gc, mean_q

  return par.map(encode_read, reads, quals)

docs.title: 2. Single-pass multi-channel alignment pileup
docs.text:
All six par.scatter_add channels (A/C/G/T counts, Phred quality sum, reverse strand count) share ref_pos, so scatter fusion merges them into one thread-privatized pass (IndexScatter: 6 → 1):

@par.jit
def single_pass_pileup(ref_pos, base_code, phred_q, is_rev, contig_len):
  """Accumulate A/C/G/T counts, quality sums, and reverse-strand counts across
  aligned base observations in one keyed IndexScatter traversal."""
  # All six histograms share ref_pos, so Parakeet fuses them into one pass.
  cnt_a = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, (base_code == Base.A).astype(np.int64))
  cnt_c = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, (base_code == Base.C).astype(np.int64))
  cnt_g = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, (base_code == Base.G).astype(np.int64))
  cnt_t = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, (base_code == Base.T).astype(np.int64))
  qual_sum = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, phred_q.astype(np.int64))
  rev_cnt = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, is_rev.astype(np.int64))
  return cnt_a, cnt_c, cnt_g, cnt_t, qual_sum, rev_cnt

docs.title: 3. 2048-bit Morgan fingerprint Tanimoto screening
docs.text:
Compares query fingerprints (N, 32) against a library (M, 32) of packed uint64 bitvectors using par.popcount, par.allpairs, and an ordered par.fold (preserving first-index ties without allocating an N × M matrix):

class BestHit(NamedTuple):
  sim: np.float32
  index: np.int64


def better_hit(left, right):
  # Highest Tanimoto similarity wins; ties preserve the first library compound.
  return right if right.sim > left.sim else left


@par.jit
def tanimoto_nearest_hit(queries, library):
  """Find the closest library compound per query over packed uint64 fingerprints
  (N, W) x (M, W) using tiled pairwise folds with zero N x M allocation."""
  pop_q = np.sum(par.popcount(queries), axis=1)
  pop_l = np.sum(par.popcount(library), axis=1)

  inter = par.allpairs(lambda q_row, l_row: np.sum(par.popcount(q_row & l_row)), queries, library)
  denom = pop_q[:, None] + pop_l[None, :] - inter
  sim = np.where(denom > 0, inter.astype(np.float32) / np.maximum(denom, 1).astype(np.float32), np.float32(0.0))
  return par.fold(BestHit, better_hit, sim, axis=1, indexed=True, emit=lambda hit: hit.index)

docs.title: 4. 3D protein coordinate RBF message passing
docs.text:
Pairwise radial-basis-function smoothing over 3D residue coordinates (N, 3) uses the same rescaled-monoid tiling as softmax attention—zero O(N²) buffers and directly differentiable through par.grad:

@par.jit
def protein_rbf_message_passing(coords, features, neg_inv_2sigma2):
  """3D radial-basis-function message passing over residue coordinates (N, 3).

  Fuses into online (m, l, O) monoidal tiles with zero N x N materialization.
  """
  d2 = np.sum((coords[:, None, :] - coords[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2.0), axis=-1)
  s = d2 * neg_inv_2sigma2
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ features


def protein_rbf_loss(coords, features, targets, neg_inv_2sigma2):
  pred = protein_rbf_message_passing(coords, features, neg_inv_2sigma2)
  diff = pred - targets
  return np.mean(diff * diff)


protein_coord_grad = par.grad(protein_rbf_loss, argnum=0)

docs.title: 5. Banded Smith-Waterman and DNA state-space scan
docs.text:
Two-row banded Smith-Waterman stays in O(M) L1 scratch, while 1D DNA exponential recurrences rewrite automatically into Law 4 chunkwise parallel scans:

@par.jit
def banded_smith_waterman(seq_a, seq_b, match_score, mismatch_pen, gap_pen, band_width):
  """Banded Smith-Waterman local alignment score over sequences.

  Keeps only two O(M) score rows in cache and restricts columns to |j - i| <= band_width.
  """
  n, m = len(seq_a), len(seq_b)
  prev = np.zeros(m + 1, dtype=np.float32)
  curr = np.zeros(m + 1, dtype=np.float32)
  best = np.float32(0.0)
  for i in range(1, n + 1):
    ai = seq_a[i - 1]
    j_lo = max(1, i - band_width)
    j_hi = min(m, i + band_width)
    for j in range(j_lo, j_hi + 1):
      sub = match_score if ai == seq_b[j - 1] else mismatch_pen
      v = max(np.float32(0.0), prev[j - 1] + sub, prev[j] + gap_pen, curr[j - 1] + gap_pen)
      curr[j] = v
      best = max(best, v)
    prev[j_lo : j_hi + 1] = curr[j_lo : j_hi + 1]
    curr[j_lo : j_hi + 1] = 0.0
  return best


@par.jit
def dna_ssm_scan(decay, signal):
  """Exponential state-space scan along a DNA track (L,).

  Compiled via chunkwise parallel affine prefix scan (TileScan).
  """
  out = np.empty_like(signal)
  s = np.float32(0.0)
  for t in range(len(decay)):
    s = decay[t] * s + signal[t]
    out[t] = s
  return out

docs.title: 7. Long-read RNA alignment & quantification
docs.text:
Inspired by Rob Patro's COMBINE lab tools (SSHash, Piscem, Spearfish, and Oarfish), examples/patro_longread_rna.py implements a full long-read RNA aligner and isoform quantifier in ~250 lines of compiled Python/NumPy:

  1. Unitig collapse + SSHash minimizer index (build_unitig_sshash_index): collapses isoforms into maximal shared unitigs in CSR arrays with a FrozenHashTable mapping sparse minimizers to unitig buckets.
  2. Streaming unitig contiguity + Spearfish delta-mapping (stream_map_long_reads): extends Maximal Exact Matches along unitigs in O(1)/base (skipping hash lookups), projects anchors to isoforms via CSR postings, chains co-linear diagonals, and keeps competitive isoforms within delta_frac.
  3. Oarfish-style coverage-aware EM (oarfish_em_quantify): compiled EM over compatibility sets weighted by alignment score and effective length.

On 80 human Ensembl cDNA isoforms (TP53, PKM, MAPT, ACTB; 225,539 raw bp), unitig collapse shrinks the reference 9.7× (23,247 bp across 231 unitigs), the SSHash fast path skips hash probes on 92.2% of bases, multicore mapping sustains 548.6 Mbp/s on Apple M1 Pro, and Oarfish EM reaches Pearson r = 0.965 against ground truth.

docs.title: 8. Streaming I/O, BGZF inflate, and compiler scope
docs.text:
Parakeet intentionally keeps file descriptors, container framing, and streaming I/O syscalls outside @par.jit so compiled kernels stay small, portable, and GPU-safe. Because compiled functions release the Python GIL, disk/codec work overlaps cleanly with compute:

  • Double-buffered I/O + compute: a background reader thread decompresses slabs (isal, zlib-ng, libdeflate, or pysam) into pinned uint8 / RaggedArray buffers while Parakeet processes the previous slab across CPU cores or on GPU (reserve 1–2 CPU cores for the reader on CPU-only hosts via PARAKEET_NUM_THREADS).
  • Block-parallel BGZF inflate fits inside @par.jit: because BGZF splits .bam / .fastq.gz files into independent ≤ 64 KiB blocks with known uncompressed sizes, examples/bgzf_and_streaming_io.py compiles a full RFC-1951 DEFLATE inflater across all blocks in parallel. On 20,000 FASTQ reads (6.31 MB raw, 97 blocks, Apple M1 Pro):
  • Raw inflate: Python gzip (1T) 226 MB/s vs. Parakeet BGZF 1T 203 MB/s vs. Parakeet BGZF multicore 1,579 MB/s (7.0×).
  • Decompress + FASTQ QC: sequential gzip + QC 168 MB/s vs. overlapped double-buffered zlib + QC 341 MB/s (2.0×) vs. Parakeet parallel BGZF + QC 906 MB/s (5.4×).
  • Use native codecs for single-stream gzip/zstd: single-stream DEFLATE has a serial 32 KiB sliding-window dependency with no data parallelism—feed decompressed uint8 slabs from isa-l/libdeflate/zstd into Parakeet.

docs.title: Compiler & language ergonomics
docs.text:
• Direct string sequences: Passing list[str] or list[bytes] to @par.jit packs equal-length ASCII strings into a 2D uint8 array (N, L) and variable-length strings into a RaggedArray[uint8].
  • Single-character ASCII comparisons & constant char-dict LUTs: Expressions like ch == "G", seq == "C", "A" <= ch <= "Z", and ch in "CG" compile directly against uint8 bytes. Constant single-char dictionaries (BASE_CODE = {"A": Base.A, ...}) lower BASE_CODE[seq] and BASE_CODE.get(ch, 4) into a static 256-entry L1-resident lookup table.
  • Multi-output & ragged par.map: Mapped functions can return tuples of scalars and/or fixed-shape arrays (unboxed into one fused parallel loop) and map directly over RaggedArray inputs.

docs.title: Bioinformatics, streaming I/O, and batched linear algebra
docs.text:
• Block-parallel BGZF inflate & overlapped FASTQ streaming (examples/bgzf_and_streaming_io.py): Full compiled RFC-1951 DEFLATE decoder (stored, fixed Huffman, and dynamic Huffman with a 9-bit fast LUT + LZ77) running in parallel across BGZF blocks (1,579 MB/s multicore inflate on Apple M1 Pro, 7.0x faster than Python gzip), paired with a double-buffered overlapped zlib + GIL-free Parakeet FASTQ QC pipeline (341 MB/s overlapped vs. 168 MB/s sequential, 906 MB/s with Parakeet BGZF + QC).
  • Batched 3D np.linalg.* & new solvers (parakeet/lib/linalg_lib.py): Added np.linalg.eigvalsh, np.linalg.pinv, np.linalg.lstsq, and batched 3D (B, M, N) support via par.map for cholesky, det, solve, inv, qr, eigh, eigvalsh, svd, and pinv.
  • Differentiable protein backbone dihedrals (examples/bio_algorithms.py): Added vectorized Ramachandran backbone_dihedrals(N, CA, C) returning (phi, psi, omega) torsion angles, verified with par.grad.
  • Simplified Pythonic examples: Rewrote C-style loops, magic ASCII numbers, and explicit par.parfor calls across examples/bio_gallery.py, examples/bio_algorithms.py, examples/patro_longread_rna.py, examples/cudatree_gbdt.py, and examples/complex_fft_and_fasta.py.

docs.title: 1.8.0 (November 26, 2026)
docs.text: Compiled np.linalg matrix decompositions and solvers, seven classic bioinformatics algorithms, a Rob Patro-style SSHash + Spearfish + Oarfish long-read RNA aligner and quantifier, and published head-to-head bioinformatics benchmarks (closing #46).

docs.title: Compiled np.linalg decompositions and solvers
docs.text: • parakeet/lib/linalg_lib.py: Pure compiled implementations (zero external LAPACK dependency, callable inside par.parfor, supporting both float32 and float64) for np.linalg.cholesky, np.linalg.det, np.linalg.solve (1D and 2D RHS), np.linalg.inv, np.linalg.qr (Householder reduced and complete), np.linalg.eigh (cyclic Jacobi, UPLO="L"/"U"), and np.linalg.svd (one-sided Hestenes Jacobi, square/tall/wide, full_matrices, compute_uv).

docs.title: Bioinformatics algorithms, long-read RNA alignment, and head-to-head benchmarks
docs.text:
• Classic bioinformatics suite (examples/bio_algorithms.py): 3-state affine-gap Gotoh alignment + traceback to RLE CIGAR, multi-word uint64 Myers bit-vector edit distance, O(N) circular monotone-deque minimizer sketching, FM-index / BWT backward search over RaggedArray[uint8], par.flatmap CIGAR expansion, profile HMM Viterbi + Forward-Backward posterior decoding, and Kabsch 3D protein superposition & RMSD using compiled np.linalg.svd and np.linalg.det.
  • Long-read RNA alignment & quantification (examples/patro_longread_rna.py): SSHash-style streaming k-mer lookup over collapsed unitigs with FrozenHashTable sparse minimizer buckets, Spearfish shared-anchor projection and delta-mapping, and compiled Oarfish coverage-aware EM. On 80 real human Ensembl isoforms (TP53, PKM, MAPT, ACTB), achieves 9.7x unitig collapse, 92.2% hash-lookup skip rate, 548.6 Mbp/s multicore mapping on Apple M1 Pro, and EM Pearson r = 0.965.
  • Head-to-head bioinformatics benchmarks (benchmarks/bio_head_to_head.py): Replicate median + IQR comparison against edlib, Biopython, Biotite, RDKit, and NumPy, published in docs/release-benchmarks.md and docs/bioinformatics.md alongside the overlapped CPU I/O and decompression architecture notes.

docs.title: 1.7.0 (November 25, 2026)
docs.text: Adaptive 3-tier ragged parallelism, fused segmented 2D histograms with histogram subtraction, parallel ragged sample partitioning, and an end-to-end CudaTree-style adaptive BFS -> DFS GBDT tree builder and benchmark (closing #82 and #83).

docs.title: Irregular tree & ragged parallelism primitives
docs.text:
• par.partition_by_size(offsets, block_thresh=1024, warp_thresh=64) and par.segmented_parfor(body, offsets, ...): Classifies CSR segments into heavy, medium, and light work-size tiers so skewed power-law distributions (such as 1 giant node alongside thousands of tiny leaves) dispatch cleanly across CPU, multicore, Apple Metal, and CUDA without warp/SIMD-group starvation.
  • par.segmented_histogram2d(node_ids, bins, grads, hess, n_nodes, n_bins): Single-pass fused 2D (grad, hess, count) scatter-add over (node_id, bin_id) via IndexScatter, pairing directly with histogram subtraction (large_child = parent - small_child) to cut histogram work by up to 2x.
  • par.ragged_partition(sample_ids, offsets, goes_left): Parallel stable partitioning of active CSR sample-index frontiers into left/right child segments on CPU, multicore, Apple Metal, and CUDA.
  • CudaTree adaptive BFS -> DFS GBDT example & benchmark: Added examples/cudatree_gbdt.py (level-wise BFS with histogram subtraction handing off small subtrees to a single fused thread-per-subtree DFS kernel using par.fixed_list scratch) and benchmarks/tree_models.py (median + IQR benchmark on balanced and skewed datasets).

docs.title: 1.6.0 (November 25, 2026)
docs.text: Unboxed complex64/complex128 arithmetic and Wirtinger AD, plus compiled byte/ASCII parsing helpers (split_bytes, parse_int64, parse_float32, parse_float64) for FASTA/CSV ingestion (Python Semantics Wave 3, closing #81).

docs.title: Unboxed complex64 and complex128
docs.text:
• Zero-copy (re, im) lowering: np.complex64, np.complex128, and Python complex values lower cleanly onto pairs of real float32/float64 views and scalar expressions, working out of the box across CPU, multicore, Apple Metal (complex64), and CUDA without IR or backend changes.
  • Complex math and linear algebra: Supports +, -, *, /, **, ==, !=, abs, conj/conjugate, .real, .imag, np.angle, np.exp, np.log, np.sqrt, np.sin, np.cos, np.matmul/@, np.dot, np.vdot, np.sum, np.mean, np.cumsum, np.where, np.concatenate, np.stack, indexing/slicing, and in-place updates with NEP 50 promotion.
  • Wirtinger automatic differentiation: par.grad, par.value_and_grad, and par.jvp differentiate real-valued losses over complex64/complex128 arrays automatically.

docs.title: Byte and ASCII parsing helpers
docs.text:
• par.split_bytes(buf, sep, skip_empty=False): Data-parallel delimiter splitting of uint8 / bytes buffers into RaggedArray[uint8] with zero PyObject allocation.
  • par.parse_int64, par.parse_float32, par.parse_float64: Compiled ASCII integer and floating-point parsers (with optional signs, decimals, and exponents) operating on single uint8 slices or in parallel over RaggedArray[uint8].
  • New runnable example: Added examples/complex_fft_and_fasta.py (Cooley-Tukey radix-2 FFT, spectral filter Wirtinger gradient, and compiled FASTA/CSV byte ingestion).

docs.title: 1.5.0 (November 25, 2026)
docs.text: Local Python lists, GPU-safe fixed-capacity scratch buffers, dynamic-shape array/ragged loop rebinding, and zero-allocation itertools combinators (Python Semantics Wave 2, closing #80).

docs.title: Lists, growable CPU vectors, & GPU scratch stacks
docs.text:
• Compile-time static list: Straight-line and unrolled outs = [] with .append(), .extend(), .pop(), .clear(), indexing/slicing, and consumption by np.stack, np.concatenate, np.array, and RaggedArray.from_sequences lowers away before IR emission and composes seamlessly with par.grad.
  • Runtime growable CPU list[T]: Lists mutated inside runtime for/while loops or dynamic if branches automatically promote to a refcounted homogeneous growable buffer (buf, len, cap) with geometric doubling and zero-copy conversion to ArrayVal (par.config.verify=True clean).
  • par.fixed_list(capacity, dtype): Fixed-capacity stack-allocated scratch buffer (ir.Alloc(..., stack=True)) emitted natively as thread-local stack arrays on CPU, multicore, CUDA, and Apple Metal with zero malloc and runtime bounds/capacity checks.
  • Dynamic-shape loop rebinding: Verified runtime shape rebinding for both ArrayVal (e.g., arr = arr[arr > thresh]) and RaggedArray across while and for loops under par.config.verify=True.
  • Static itertools & generators: Zero-allocation compilation for itertools.pairwise, itertools.islice, itertools.chain, itertools.product, and itertools.batched in for loops and generator expressions (sum(...), np.array(...)).

docs.title: 1.4.0 (November 25, 2026)
docs.text: Broader idiomatic Python semantics lowered cleanly at elaboration time with zero PyObject overhead: non-frozen @dataclass records with pure methods, @property, __call__, and functional field rebinding; full structural match/case destructuring; compile-time isinstance/hasattr/getattr dead-branch pruning; and *args/**kwargs, functools.partial, and operator.* call ergonomics (Python Semantics Wave 1, closing #79).

docs.title: Non-frozen @dataclass, methods & @property
docs.text:
• Non-frozen @dataclass records: Both frozen and regular @dataclass objects compile to unboxed compile-time records across @par.jit, par.grad, and par.jvp (with discrete metadata fields treated as zero-tangent static leaves).
  • Functional local field rebinding: obj.x = new_x, nested obj.a.b = v, and augmented updates obj.x += v rebuild the compile-time record chain functionally (value semantics, zero heap mutation); including across loops and branches.
  • Pure methods, @property, @staticmethod, @classmethod, & __call__: Methods and properties on @dataclass and NamedTuple records inline like ordinary helper functions; bound methods on records can also be passed directly from Python into @par.jit and par.map.

docs.title: Structural match/case, isinstance/hasattr, & call ergonomics
docs.text:
• Extended structural match/case: Added MatchMapping (case {"k": v, **rest}:), starred array patterns (case [first, *mid, last]:), and class patterns for non-frozen dataclasses, RaggedArray, np.ndarray, dict, and tuple.
  • Compile-time isinstance, hasattr, & getattr: Resolved statically against the specialization key (including Python 3.10+ union types A | B, user dataclasses, NamedTuple, and RaggedArray) with guaranteed dead-branch pruning.
  • Call ergonomics: Full **kwargs collection and **d unpacking, functools.partial (both inside @par.jit and passed from Python), and operator.* callables (operator.add, operator.mul, operator.itemgetter, operator.attrgetter, etc.) including associative par.reduce/par.scan combiners.
  • New runnable gallery example: Added examples/protein_and_layers.py (ProteinBackbone + MLPBlock with polymorphic dense/RaggedArray dispatch and reverse-mode AD).

docs.title: 1.3.0 (November 25, 2026)
docs.text: Composable forward-mode, general reverse-mode, and higher-order automatic differentiation (jvp, vjp, linearize, linear_transpose, hvp, jacfwd, jacrev, hessian, @custom_jvp), zero-$O(T^2)$ rematerialized attention JVP/HVP, idiomatic np.add.at and for-loop scatter lifting, and a documentation and examples overhaul (AD Upgrade Wave 2, closing #76, #77, and #78).

docs.title: Forward-mode AD, general VJPs & linear transposes
docs.text:
• par.jvp & @par.custom_jvp: Symbolic forward-mode differentiation over scalars, arrays, matmul/einsum, reductions (tie-averaged min/max, zero-safe prod), scans, folds, map, gather/scatter, if/else, runtime for/while loops (in $O(1)$ extra memory), NamedTuple / frozen @dataclass records, and RaggedArrays.
  • General non-scalar par.vjp, par.linearize, & par.linear_transpose: Full reverse-mode pullbacks for array, tuple, record, and RaggedArray outputs, plus exact linear operator transposes satisfying ⟨JVP(x; v), u⟩ == ⟨v, VJP(x; u)⟩.
  • Higher-order AD (par.hvp, par.jacfwd, par.jacrev, par.hessian): Forward-over-reverse Hessian-vector products across MLPs, LayerNorm, checkpointed for loops, and FlashAttention. Also lifted reverse-over-reverse grad(grad(...)) cliffs for np.stack, np.cumsum, gather indexing, scatter-add, and scalar 1-to-1 par.map.

docs.title: Composable algebraic AD & indexing adjoints
docs.text:
• Zero-$O(T^2)$ attention JVP & HVP: Fused dual (S, dS) -> (O, dO) monoidal tiling and parallel rematerialized HVP tangent emission drop all quadratic $O(T^2)$ allocations during both par.jvp and par.hvp (reported by par.show_rewrite).
  • Composable ALGEBRAIC_AD_RULES registry: Unified FlashAttention, Cut Cross-Entropy, softmax, and LayerNorm / RMSNorm rematerialization rules and enabled algebraic tape optimization inside checkpointed runtime for loops.
  • topk, sort, FrozenHashTable, & SortedIndex AD: Added reverse-mode and forward-mode differentiation for par.topk / par.topk_fold, np.sort, FrozenHashTable.get, and SortedIndex.get.
  • Multi-store vertical fusion fix: Hardened match_single_output_map and match_single_output_scan to reject multi-store prefixes, fixing a compiler bug exposed by fused primal+tangent IndexMaps.

docs.title: Idiomatic scatter lowering & documentation overhaul
docs.text:
• np.add.at and for-loop scatter lifting: np.add.at(out, idx, vals) and canonical for i in range(n): out[idx[i]] += vals[i] loops (including multi-histogram bodies sharing an index binding b = bin_ids[i]) now lift directly to IndexScatter, fuse sibling histograms into one privatized traversal, and differentiate cleanly under both grad and jvp.
  • Consistent NumPy idioms & pedagogical gallery: Standardized docs and examples on np.* helpers (np.minimum, np.add, np.add.at, etc.) alongside @par.jit / par.* operators, replaced bare Law 1..6 shorthand outside docs/algebra.md with plain-English optimization descriptions, and reordered the Kernel gallery progressively from pairwise NumPy fusion to attention and end-to-end training.

docs.title: 1.2.0 (November 25, 2026)
docs.text: Major automatic differentiation upgrade: IR-level checkpointed reverse loops for runtime-bound for/while loops, par.fold, and general par.scan, plus par.stop_gradient, @par.custom_vjp, and @par.checkpoint (AD Upgrade Wave 1, closing #75 and advancing #77).

docs.title: Reverse-mode AD through runtime & long loops
docs.text:
• IR-level $O(\sqrt{T})$ checkpointed reverse for loops: Loops over runtime-length ranges or arrays (for t in range(T):, for t in range(weights.shape[0]):) and long static loops (> 32 iterations) compile once to a two-level checkpointed reverse loop in IR without unrolling or recompiling per length, removing the MAX_UNROLL = 4096 cliff.
  • IR-level $O(\log T)$ checkpointed reverse while loops: Runtime-converging while loops (fixed-point solvers, adaptive ODE/relaxation steps) now differentiate through a fixed-slot (64 slots) stride-doubling online checkpoint schedule with bounded memory.
  • Checkpointed $O(\sqrt{N})$ par.fold & differentiable general par.scan: Arbitrary non-monoidal par.reduce/par.fold and 1-D par.scan now differentiate via checkpointed reverse segments without storing full $O(N)$ histories.
  • Rewrite inspection: par.show_rewrite(par.grad(...), ...) now reports AD: Checkpointed Reverse Loop when checkpointed reverse loops are emitted.

docs.title: Explicit AD control primitives
docs.text:
• par.stop_gradient(x): Zero-copy gradient barrier across scalars, arrays, tuples, RaggedArray, and records (for straight-through estimators, target networks, and stop-gradient RL losses).
  • @par.custom_vjp (.defvjp(fwd, bwd)): User-defined reverse-mode rules supporting multi-output pytree values, auxiliary residuals, and higher-order differentiation.
  • @par.checkpoint (rematerialization): Explicit activation checkpointing that re-runs the forward block during backpropagation while composing cleanly with Law 2 FlashAttention / LayerNorm rematerialization.
  • Record static metadata leaves: Non-float fields inside NamedTuple and frozen @dataclass records now pass through AD as zero-tangent static leaves.

docs.title: 1.1.0 (November 25, 2026)
docs.text: Major expansion of Parakeet's GPU schedules, algebraic data structures, scientific/bioinformatics primitives, and documentation; unified under one top-level import parakeet as par (@par.jit, par.*) interface.

docs.title: Unified namespace, docs & benchmarks
docs.text:
• Single unified parakeet namespace: Exported fold, topk, topk_fold, tanimoto_topk, ipa_attention, show_rewrite, RewriteReport, scatter, iscan, iscatter, and ifilter_reduce directly on top-level parakeet (with parakeet.dsl retained as a backward-compatible alias). Standardized examples and docs on import parakeet as par (@par.jit, par.*).
  • Reproducible benchmark figures & overhaul: Added tools/gen_benchmark_figures.py generating per-replicate scatter + IQR + median SVGs (bench-pairwise-l4.svg, bench-scaling-1nn.svg, bench-workloads-l4.svg) directly from docs/assets/colab-l4-0dcb7d5.json, reorganized the Benchmarks page by workload category, connected README.md directly to runnable implementations, and updated the NYU history links (Rubinsteyn 2014 thesis, Hielscher et al. 2013 arXiv:1304.1835, HotPar '12).
  • Bioinformatics & structural biology guide: Added the Bioinformatics & structural biology gallery (examples/bio_gallery.py) and reproducible benchmark suite (benchmarks/bio_workloads.py).

docs.title: GPU schedules & matrix units
docs.text:
• Tiled GPU pairwise folds: Broadcasting NumPy and nested-map/structured par.fold exact 1-NN and inverse-distance smoothing now stream shared-memory score tiles (16 KiB/block) on CUDA and Metal with exact first-index tie and NaN semantics; 4.8× faster (2.60 ms → 0.54 ms) and 21× less global scratch (64 MiB → 3 MiB) at 1,024 × 16,384 × 32 on NVIDIA L4.
  • Hardware matrix units in monoidal kernels: Enabled Metal simdgroup_matrix and CUDA TF32 WMMA inside Law 1 rescaled-monoid kernels (FlashAttention, RBF, linear cross-entropy, nanoGPT training).
  • Device-resident GPU scans & reductions: Kept GPU prefix scans, small GPU reductions, and extrema values device-resident without host round-trips.

docs.title: New algebraic primitives & data structures
docs.text:
• First-class RaggedArray (CSR) & segmented operators: RaggedArray, segment_ids, segmented_map, segmented_reduce, segmented_scan, segmented_softmax, and differentiable varlen_flash_attention with ragged reverse-mode AD (par.grad preserves offsets structurally).
  • 1-to-K ragged compaction (IndexExpand): Added par.flatmap and par.filter_pairs (two-pass count → prefix-sum → emit) with dead-output elimination and AD gather support.
  • Parallel sorting, search & lookup tables: Parallel radix sort / argsort / unique, fusible searchsorted, SortedIndex, and static open-addressed FrozenHashTable.
  • 3D spatial pruning & block-sparse attention (Law 5 generalized): morton_order, 3D AABB spatial_cutoff_sum, and CSR BlockMask block_sparse_attention with forward + backward AD.
  • 2D / banded semiring DP (IndexWavefront): Added par.wavefront, par.batched_wavefront, and Law 2 checkpointed differentiable par.soft_align (Smith-Waterman / Needleman-Wunsch / soft-DTW).
  • Vector-valued Carry folds & pair-biased / IPA attention: Multi-slot Carry folds powering exact par.topk, par.topk_fold, par.tanimoto_topk, and Law 1+2 par.ipa_attention.
  • Zero-copy bytes, bitops & Python ergonomics: Zero-copy uint8 bytes / mmap inputs, popcount/clz/ctz/rotl/rotr/bswap, bf16_to_f32 / f32_to_bf16, IntEnum, scalar match/case, frozen @dataclass dataclasses.replace, and structured NumPy views.

docs.title: 1.0.0 (November 24, 2026)
docs.text: A ground-up rewrite for modern Python. The @jit decorator, the adverbs (map, reduce, scan, allpairs, imap, ...) and the overall idea are unchanged; everything underneath is new.

docs.title: Algebraic operators
docs.text:
• The same CPU tile schedule serves exact nearest-neighbor queries written as broadcasting NumPy or nested parallel maps. It merges a distance and index per query and preserves the first index on ties.
  • Two weighted histograms over shared bin IDs can fuse into a single traversal. Structured folds accept tuples and named records with a user-defined merge.
  • Algebraic rewrites cover online normalized sums, their gradients, reassociation of contractions, and chunked affine scans. The rewrite inspector shows which passes fired for a given function and input.
  • The gallery includes runnable examples. The release benchmarks compare five workloads with general-purpose and specialist implementations on a four-vCPU worker and an NVIDIA A10.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• grad and value_and_grad: reverse-mode differentiation as an adverb. Element-wise operators, reductions, matrix products, views, map and allpairs with your own functions all have derivative rules; loops of known length are unrolled; anything without a rule raises instead of returning a wrong gradient. examples/nanogpt.py and examples/convnet.py train with it.
  • More of grad: cumsum, sort, einsum, stacks of matrices, folds with any function, and if statements on run-time conditions (both branches run, results are selected). The derivative of a map runs in parallel.
  • A middle end: elaboration now produces operator statements (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, printed by spec.operators) and a pipeline of passes rewrites them before they become loops. Tiling is one such pass, a pattern match on the IR instead of a trial elaboration; vertical fusion (Map→Map including matmul epilogues, Scan→Map into emit, Map→Filter, Map→Reduce), filter fusion (Filter→Filter and Filter→Reduce: np.sum(x[x > 0]) is one loop and allocates nothing), sibling fusion (x.min(), x.max() and np.sin(x), np.cos(x) each share one loop), reduction interchange (np.sum(X, axis=0) becomes L1-tiled contiguous SIMD loops), and dead-operator elimination all run at this level; find_broken_transform bisects the pass list; config.skip_transforms switches passes off.
  • General operators: reduce, scan and filter take several arrays with map= (and emit=); np.einsum; @ on stacks; reductions over several axes in one pass; tiling for maps of any rank.
  • Parallel primitives: prefix scans (cumsum), filters (x[mask], nonzero) and argmin/argmax run in parallel, on CPUs and GPUs.
  • GPU: arrays stay on the device between the loops of one call; a loop is sent to the device by the work in it, not its element count.
  • BLAS: float matrix products call the BLAS NumPy uses.
  • Tiling: two-dimensional maps of reductions (@, allpairs distances, ...) run a cache-sized tile at a time with their reductions jammed 2×4. A 1024×1024 matrix product is 2× faster on one core and 3× on all of them.
  • np.sort and np.argsort take axis and sort every lane in parallel (N-d input used to be flattened without saying so).
  • The dimensions of an array argument can be compile-time constants when the code needs them to be (range(w.shape[0]) in a loop that must be unrolled).
  • parakeet.macro and parakeet.find_broken_transform are back, and the code is laid out in frontend/, syntax/, transforms/ and lib/ again.
  • Faster compiles for large functions: identical loop bodies are compiled once.
  • Checked on real NVIDIA hardware. The whole suite passes with every parallel loop forced onto a Tesla T4 (tools/colab_job.py, run on demand with runplz colab; not part of CI).
  • Reads like Parakeet again: two-space indentation, parakeet.prims and parakeet.ndtypes, and the 0.x helpers typed_repr, specialize, run_python_fn, openmp_available, rank/size/shape, plus the old config.opt_fusion / config.print_* option names.

  • Fixed: two arguments of one GPU kernel that view the same memory now share a device buffer (previously one of them could read a truncated copy).

  • Python 3.11+ and NumPy 2, no dependencies besides NumPy and a C compiler (the dsltools, appdirs, llvmpy and PyCUDA dependencies are gone).

  • New frontend. Functions are elaborated directly into a typed loop IR: calls are inlined, closures/tuples/slices are resolved at compile time, and array expressions are fused into their consumers.
  • Backends: sequential C; multi-core through a built-in thread pool, OpenMP or Grand Central Dispatch; Apple GPUs through Metal; NVIDIA GPUs through CUDA (CuPy/NVRTC, no nvcc needed). GPU backends fall back to the CPU per loop, with a warning that says why.
  • NumPy-exact typing (NEP 50): result dtypes match NumPy, including the treatment of Python scalars.
  • Safety: bounds checks, shape checks, division and domain checks raise the same exceptions NumPy/Python would; compile errors carry the source location and the chain of inlined calls; reference-counted temporaries are freed eagerly (no more leaks in loops).
  • Much larger language subset: early return, break/continue, while, keyword/default/*args arguments, walrus, assert/raise, boolean-mask and integer-array indexing (reads and writes), in-place operators with NumPy aliasing semantics, 0-d and empty arrays, all integer/float dtypes.
  • Much larger library: ~200 NumPy functions and methods, np.random (a counter-based generator that is reproducible in parallel and on GPUs), sorting, math, and most numeric builtins.
  • Globals and closure variables are read at call time (no stale constants); arguments that must be compile-time constants (such as axis) are specialised on demand.
  • Compiled modules are cached on disk and shared between processes.
  • parakeet.config, parakeet.options(...), PARAKEET_* environment variables, f.specialize(...).ir/.source/.kernels, available_backends().

Anything outside Parakeet's supported subset fails at specialization time as a subclass of parakeet.CompileError:

docs.text:
Compiled code raises standard Python exceptions with the failing source line, even from inside parallel CPU loops and GPU kernels (freeing any temporary allocations first):

@par.jit
def third(x):
  return x[2]


third(np.zeros(2))
# IndexError: index 2 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 2
#   raised by compiled code at demo.py:5 (in third)
Condition Exception Out-of-bounds index IndexError Broadcast mismatch, bad reshape, ragged map output, empty unseeded reduction, writing to a read-only array ValueError Scalar //, %, or / by zero on Python numbers ZeroDivisionError Failed assert AssertionError Out of memory MemoryError

NumPy array division matches NumPy: integer division by zero yields 0, and float division by zero yields inf / nan.

docs.title: Kernel gallery
docs.text:
Parakeet compiles NumPy expressions, Python loops, and explicit data-parallel operators (par.map, par.allpairs, par.fold, par.imap, par.ireduce, par.scatter_add) through one @par.jit decorator. Where a section has tabs, each spelling compiles to the same fused, tiled schedule.

Every snippet below is included verbatim from examples/algebraic_gallery.py and verified by python -m examples.algebraic_gallery. See also Train nanoGPT and Bioinformatics & structural biology.

from typing import NamedTuple
import numpy as np
import parakeet as par

docs.title: Exact nearest neighbor
docs.text:
Find the closest reference vector among R references for each of Q queries in Rᴰ. Naive NumPy allocates a Q × R distance matrix (64 MiB at Q = 1,024, R = 16,384); Parakeet streams 16 KiB tiles in L1/SRAM and keeps NumPy's exact first-index rule on ties and NaNs.

Broadcasting NumPyNested par.map and np.argminpar.allpairs and structured par.fold 
@par.jit
def nearest_numpy(queries, references):
  delta = queries[:, None, :] - references[None, :, :]
  return np.argmin(np.sum(delta ** np.float32(2), axis=2), axis=1)

def squared_distance(query, reference):
  return np.sum((query - reference) ** np.float32(2))



@par.jit
def exact_1nn(x_query, x_ref):
  """Exact nearest-neighbor index per query row."""
  return par.map(
    lambda query: np.argmin(par.map(lambda reference: squared_distance(query, reference), x_ref)),
    x_query,
  )

def squared_distance(query, reference):
  return np.sum((query - reference) ** np.float32(2))



class Winner(NamedTuple):
  distance: np.float32
  index: np.int64


def first_minimum(left, right):
  # Keep the first NaN. Among finite values, replace only on strict improvement.
  right_wins = np.isnan(right.distance) or right.distance < left.distance
  return right if right_wins and not np.isnan(left.distance) else left


@par.jit
def nearest_fold(queries, references):
  scores = par.allpairs(squared_distance, queries, references)
  return par.fold(Winner, first_minimum, scores, axis=1, indexed=True, emit=lambda winner: winner.index)

All three spellings compile to the same tiled pairwise schedule on CPU, Metal, and CUDA. Compare timings and scratch memory.

docs.title: Inverse-distance smoothing
docs.text:
Swap the fold state from (min_dist, idx) to (weight_sum, weighted_sum) to smooth targets with weight w[i, j] = 1 / (1 + ‖q[i] − r[j]‖²) in a single tiled pass:

Broadcasting NumPypar.allpairs and par.fold 
@par.jit
def smooth_numpy(queries, references, observations):
  observations = observations.reshape(references.shape[0])
  delta = queries[:, None, :] - references[None, :, :]
  weights = 1 / (1 + np.sum(delta ** np.float32(2), axis=2))
  return np.sum(weights * observations, axis=1) / np.sum(weights, axis=1)

def squared_distance(query, reference):
  return np.sum((query - reference) ** np.float32(2))



class WeightedSum(NamedTuple):
  weight: np.float32
  weighted_value: np.float32


def add_sums(left, right):
  return WeightedSum(left.weight + right.weight, left.weighted_value + right.weighted_value)


@par.jit
def smooth_fold(queries, references, observations):
  values = observations.reshape(references.shape[0])
  scores = par.allpairs(squared_distance, queries, references)

  def contribution(distance_squared, ref_index):
    weight = 1 / (1 + distance_squared)
    return WeightedSum(weight, weight * values[ref_index])

  def weighted_mean(total):
    return total.weighted_value / total.weight

  return par.fold(contribution, add_sums, scores, axis=1, indexed=True, emit=weighted_mean)

docs.title: Gaussian kernel regression
docs.text:
Nadaraya-Watson smoothing weights references by exp(-gamma * ‖q[i] − x[j]‖²). Law 1 rescaled-monoid tiling streams tiles without allocating an N × M weight matrix:

@par.jit
def rbf_kernel_regression(x_query, x_train, y_train, neg_gamma):
  d2 = np.sum((x_query[:, None, :] - x_train[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2.0), axis=-1)
  s = d2 * neg_gamma
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ y_train

docs.title: Histograms and tree splits
docs.text:
Gradient-boosted trees accumulate gradients and Hessians into feature bins and pick the split with maximum gain. All four spellings below lower to O(N) IndexScatter and fuse both histograms into one thread-privatized pass:

Declarative comprehensionNumPy np.add.atPython for loopExplicit par.scatter_add

Inverts [np.sum(grads[bin_ids == b]) for b in range(nbins)] automatically from O(nbins · N) to one O(N) fused histogram pass:

@par.jit
def gbdt_best_split_comprehension(bin_ids, grads, hess, nbins, reg_lambda):
  """Declarative pull-style comprehension inverted to one fused O(N) scatter."""
  g_hist = np.array([np.sum(grads[bin_ids == b]) for b in range(nbins)])
  h_hist = np.array([np.sum(hess[bin_ids == b]) for b in range(nbins)])
  g_left = np.cumsum(g_hist)
  h_left = np.cumsum(h_hist)
  g_right = g_left[nbins - 1] - g_left
  h_right = h_left[nbins - 1] - h_left
  gain = (g_left * g_left) / (h_left + reg_lambda) + (g_right * g_right) / (h_right + reg_lambda)
  best_bin = np.argmax(gain)
  return best_bin, gain[best_bin]

@par.jit
def gbdt_best_split_numpy(bin_ids, grads, hess, nbins, reg_lambda):
  """Return the split bin with the highest gain and the gain at that bin."""
  g_hist = np.zeros(nbins, dtype=np.float32)
  h_hist = np.zeros(nbins, dtype=np.float32)
  np.add.at(g_hist, bin_ids, grads)
  np.add.at(h_hist, bin_ids, hess)
  g_left = np.cumsum(g_hist)
  h_left = np.cumsum(h_hist)
  g_right = g_left[nbins - 1] - g_left
  h_right = h_left[nbins - 1] - h_left
  gain = (g_left * g_left) / (h_left + reg_lambda) + (g_right * g_right) / (h_right + reg_lambda)
  best_bin = np.argmax(gain)
  return best_bin, gain[best_bin]

Lifts independent indexed += updates into one fused parallel histogram:

@par.jit
def gbdt_best_split_loop(bin_ids, grads, hess, nbins, reg_lambda):
  """Same histogram split written with a plain Python accumulation loop."""
  g_hist = np.zeros(nbins, dtype=np.float32)
  h_hist = np.zeros(nbins, dtype=np.float32)
  for i in range(len(bin_ids)):
    b = bin_ids[i]
    g_hist[b] += grads[i]
    h_hist[b] += hess[i]
  g_left = np.cumsum(g_hist)
  h_left = np.cumsum(h_hist)
  g_right = g_left[nbins - 1] - g_left
  h_right = h_left[nbins - 1] - h_left
  gain = (g_left * g_left) / (h_left + reg_lambda) + (g_right * g_right) / (h_right + reg_lambda)
  best_bin = np.argmax(gain)
  return best_bin, gain[best_bin]

@par.jit
def gbdt_best_split(bin_ids, grads, hess, nbins, reg_lambda):
  """Return the split bin with the highest gain and the gain at that bin."""
  g_hist = par.scatter_add(nbins, bin_ids, grads)
  h_hist = par.scatter_add(nbins, bin_ids, hess)
  g_left = np.cumsum(g_hist)
  h_left = np.cumsum(h_hist)
  g_tot = g_left[nbins - 1]
  h_tot = h_left[nbins - 1]
  g_right = g_tot - g_left
  h_right = h_tot - h_left
  gain = (g_left * g_left) / (h_left + reg_lambda) + (g_right * g_right) / (h_right + reg_lambda)
  best_bin = np.argmax(gain)
  return best_bin, gain[best_bin]

docs.title: Min-plus matrix product
docs.text:
Tropical matrix multiplication replaces (*, +) with (+, min): C[i, j] = min_r (A[i, r] + B[r, j]). Writing the index space explicitly with par.imap and par.ireduce(..., combine=np.minimum) avoids an m × n × k broadcast tensor and triggers cache and register tiling:

@par.jit
def tropical_min_plus(a, b):
  """One min-plus matrix product: C[i, j] = min_r (A[i, r] + B[r, j])."""
  m, k = a.shape
  _, n = b.shape
  return par.imap(
    lambda i, j: par.ireduce(lambda r: a[i, r] + b[r, j], k, combine=np.minimum),
    (m, n),
  )

docs.title: Exponential IIR filter
docs.text:
A plain for t in range(T): affine recurrence s = a[t] * s + b[t] rewrites via Law 4 chunkwise duality into a parallel prefix scan across CPU cores or GPU threadblocks:

@par.jit
def iir_exponential_filter(a, b):
  T = a.shape[0]
  out = np.empty_like(b)
  s = np.float32(0.0)
  for t in range(T):
    s = a[t] * s + b[t]
    out[t] = s
  return out

docs.title: Mamba-2 state-space recurrence
docs.text:
The same pass turns a 6-line bilinear matrix-state loop into division-free chunkwise GEMMs that lower directly to CPU register tiles, Metal simdgroup_matrix, and CUDA TF32 WMMA:

@par.jit
def mamba2_ssd(q, k, v, a):
  T = q.shape[0]
  out = np.empty((T, v.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
  S = np.zeros((k.shape[1], v.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
  for t in range(T):
    S = a[t] * S + k[t][:, None] * v[t][None, :]
    out[t] = q[t] @ S
  return out

docs.title: Causal attention
docs.text:
Four lines of NumPy automatically compose online monoidal tiling (no T × T matrices), tile-interval block skipping (upper triangle never loaded), and rematerialized AD under par.grad, par.jvp, and par.hvp:

@par.jit
def causal_flash_attention(q, k, v):
  T = q.shape[-2]
  idx = np.arange(T)
  mask = idx[:, None] >= idx[None, :]
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = np.where(mask, np.matmul(q, np.swapaxes(k, -1, -2)) * scale, np.float32(-1e9))
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return np.matmul(e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True), v)

Intersect the mask with (idx[:, None] - idx[None, :]) <= window for an automatic O(N · W) sliding window.

docs.title: Linear cross-entropy
docs.text:
Tiles h @ w and logsumexp over the vocabulary V without allocating an M × V logit matrix (forward and backward):

def cut_cross_entropy(h, w, targets):
  logits = h @ w
  m = np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
  z = logits - m
  lse = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(z), axis=-1))
  picked = z[np.arange(h.shape[0]), targets]
  return -np.mean(picked - lse)

docs.title: Multi-head latent attention
docs.text:
Law 3 contraction reassociation absorbs w_uk into q and defers w_uv during short-query decode so tiled attention runs directly over the compressed latent c_kv:

@par.jit
def deepseek_mla(q, c_kv, w_uk, w_uv):
  k = c_kv @ w_uk
  v = c_kv @ w_uv
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = (q @ k.T) * scale
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ v

docs.title: Grouped-query attention
docs.text:
Shared-KV head-group tiling folds the head-group axis G into the query tile so all G query heads reuse one shared-memory load of k and v:

@par.jit
def gqa_attention(q, k, v):
  # q: (B, H_kv, G, T_q, D), k, v: (B, H_kv, 1, T_kv, D)
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = np.matmul(q, np.swapaxes(k, -1, -2)) * scale
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return np.matmul(e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True), v)

docs.title: Dataclasses, methods, and polymorphic dispatch
docs.text:
@dataclass modules, pure methods, @property, __call__, and structural match/case inline completely during elaboration with zero PyObject overhead:

@dataclass
class ProteinBackbone:
  """Mutable-style @dataclass with pure methods, @property, and functional field updates."""

  coords: np.ndarray  # (N, 3, 3) for N, CA, C atoms per residue
  residue_ids: np.ndarray  # (N,) int64 metadata (zero-tangent static leaf under AD)
  chain_name: str = "A"

  @property
  def ca_coords(self):
    return self.coords[:, 1, :]

  @property
  def n_residues(self):
    return self.coords.shape[0]

  def centered(self):
    mu = np.mean(self.ca_coords, axis=0, keepdims=True)
    self.coords = self.coords - mu[:, None, :]
    return self

  def rbf_message_passing(self, features, neg_gamma):
    ca = self.ca_coords
    d2 = np.sum((ca[:, None, :] - ca[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2.0), axis=-1)
    s = d2 * neg_gamma
    e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ features


@dataclass
class MLPBlock:
  """Callable @dataclass layer with polymorphic dense/ragged dispatch."""

  w1: np.ndarray
  b1: np.ndarray
  w2: np.ndarray
  b2: np.ndarray
  name: str = "mlp"

  def __call__(self, x, *, mask=None, scale=1.0):
    if isinstance(x, RaggedArray):
      h = np.tanh(x.values @ self.w1 + self.b1)
      y = (h @ self.w2 + self.b2) * scale
      return RaggedArray(y, x.offsets)
    h = np.tanh(x @ self.w1 + self.b1)
    y = (h @ self.w2 + self.b2) * scale
    if mask is not None:
      y = np.where(mask[:, None], y, np.float32(0.0))
    return y


def apply_with_kwargs(fn, x, *args, **kwargs):
  return fn(x, *args, **kwargs)


@par.jit
def score_structure(backbone, features, block, neg_gamma, mask=None):
  bb = backbone.centered()
  msgs = bb.rbf_message_passing(features, neg_gamma)
  step = functools.partial(apply_with_kwargs, block, scale=np.float32(0.5))
  out = step(msgs, mask=mask)
  match out:
    case RaggedArray(values=vals):
      return par.reduce(operator.add, vals * vals)
    case _:
      return np.sum(out * out)
