docs.title: Compiler architecture
docs.text: Parakeet compiles a decorated Python function through four clean stages: elaboration, algebraic optimization, loop lowering, and multi-target codegen.

docs.title: 1. Specialization
docs.text:
Calling a @par.jit function classifies its arguments—array dtype, rank, contiguity/layout, scalar types, container structure, and callable identity—into a type key. Each distinct key compiles to one cached native specialization. Globals and closed-over variables are classified the same way on every call and passed as hidden arguments so compiled code never reads stale values.

When a tiled or GPU kernel queries shape divisibility or bucket bounds (for example, aligned 16-byte vector loads or tile multiples), Parakeet guards only those queried dimensions via a finite power-of-2 lattice (DimInfo(lo, hi, align)), so aligned sizes like 128, 256, 512, 1024, 4096 share one fast-path binary.

docs.title: 2. Elaboration
docs.text:
The frontend (parakeet/frontend/) is a staged interpreter that walks the Python AST with compile-time values and emits IR only for runtime work:

  • Scalars become typed SSA expressions.
  • Compile-time structures (tuples, NamedTuples, fixed-key dicts, @dataclasses, slices, functions, dtypes) dissolve completely—helper calls inline with zero Python frame or object overhead.
  • Arrays are either concrete (buffer pointer, offset, shape, strides—so views are pure integer arithmetic) or delayed (an index-to-value function that fuses into its consumer before any middle-end pass runs).

Three events trigger an automatic elaboration restart with refined information:

  1. Loop type promotion: a loop-carried variable widens (x = 0 then x += 0.5 restarts with x: float64).
  2. Eager materialization: an expensive delayed array is read more than once, read inside a loop, or invalidated by an aliasing store.
  3. Value specialization: a compile-time parameter (axis=, keepdims=, tuple length, or size-1 broadcast axis) is needed from a function argument.

Automatic differentiation (autodiff.py, jvp.py, algebraic_vjp.py) runs during elaboration: forward mode propagates symbolic tangents alongside primals, while reverse mode records operators on an algebraic tape, applies Law 2 rematerialization, and emits adjoint operators back into the same pipeline.

docs.title: 3. Middle-end passes
docs.text:
parakeet/transforms/pipeline.py runs 12 passes over the operator IR in order (parakeet.transforms.pipeline.names()). When config.verify is enabled, parakeet.verify checks types, scoping, and buffer ownership after every pass; individual passes can be disabled via config.skip_transforms.

# Pass Module Responsibility 1 dead code simplify.py Drop pure unused operators and allocations to a fixed point 2 normalize normalize.py Squeeze unit keepdims map axes and hoist row-invariant inner reductions 3 vertical fusion fusion.py Fuse Map→Map (incl. affine views/epilogues), Scan→Map, Map→Reduce/Filter/Scatter, and flatten nested maps 4 filter fusion fusion.py Merge adjacent IndexFilters and fold Filter→Reduce into zero-alloc guarded IndexReduce 5 sibling fusion fusion.py Merge sibling reductions, maps (plus CUDA disjoint-union batching), same-key scatters, and online logsumexp 6 contraction reassociation reassociate.py Reorder chained bilinear contractions by FLOP cost (incl. MLA absorption) 7 monoidal tiling monoid_tile.py Tile rescaled semiring reductions (attention, Split-K, CCE, RBF) with Law 5 tile-interval mask pruning 8 row pipeline fusion fusion.py Collapse multi-stage per-row reduction + normalization chains (LayerNorm / RMSNorm) into single-pass GPU warp pipelines 9 chunkwise scan tile_scan.py Rewrite affine and bilinear matrix-state for loops into parallel chunkwise scans 10 pairwise fold tiling pairwise_fold.py Fuse pairwise score producers into ordered CPU/GPU tile-summary folds (e.g. 1-NN) 11 reduction interchange tiling.py Hoist strided associative inner reductions outside L1 strips on CPU (PermuteReductions) 12 tiling tiling.py Emit cache/register tiles on CPU, shared-memory / matrix-unit tiles on CUDA & Metal, and single-pass CUDA atomic reductions

After these 12 passes, lowering (lowering.py) turns all operator statements into scalar ForRange loops and the single parallel loop construct, ParLoop.

docs.title: 4. Lowered IR (spec.operators and spec.ir)
docs.text:
Underneath the algebraic passes lies a typed, explicit-offset SSA IR with scoped static memory management (buffers free on scope exit; refcounting is used only when a buffer escapes).

Inspect both the pre-pass operator IR and post-lowering loop IR on any @par.jit function:

import numpy as np
import parakeet as par


@par.jit
def rms(x):
  return np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x))


spec = rms.specialize(np.ones(1024, dtype=np.float64))
print(spec.operators)  # operator IR before the 12 middle-end passes
print(spec.ir)  # lowered loop IR after all passes + lowering

Example lowered IR for rms(x):

def rms(x_1: array[float64, 1d]):
    nchunks_9: int64? = @num_chunks(x_n0_3, True)
    partials_10 = alloc(float64, nchunks_9)
    parallel[reduce] for chunk_11, (start_12, stop_13) in chunks(x_n0_3, n=nchunks_9):
        x_15: float64 = (x_1[(x_off_2 + start_12)] * x_1[(x_off_2 + start_12)])
        acc_14: float64 = x_15
        for i_16 in range((start_12 + 1), stop_13, 1):  # simd
            x_17: float64 = (x_1[(x_off_2 + i_16)] * x_1[(x_off_2 + i_16)])
            acc_14: float64 = (acc_14 + x_17)
        partials_10[chunk_11] = acc_14
    acc_8: float64 = 0.0
    for i_18 in range(0, nchunks_9, 1):
        acc_8: float64 = (acc_8 + partials_10[i_18])
    res_20: float64 = sqrt((acc_8 / float64(x_n0_3)))
    return res_20

To trace every pass that modifies a function, pass a callback to trace_passes:

from parakeet.syntax import ir

prev = None


def on_pass(stage, fn):
  global prev
  text = ir.fmt_function(fn)
  if text != prev:
    print(f"=== {stage} ===\n{text}")
    prev = text


rms.trace_passes(np.ones(1024), _trace=on_pass)

docs.title: 5. Backends and calling convention
docs.text:
All targets share one C-family scalar emitter (backends/cfamily.py) and one set of scalar math helpers (NumPy floor division/modulo, NaN-propagating min/max, RNG) so CPU, Metal, and CUDA agree bit-for-bit on integer results.

  • Host C (backends/c.py): outlines each ParLoop into a function taking a context struct (alpha-identical bodies deduplicate) and dispatches through a runtime function pointer (thread pool, OpenMP, GCD, or sequential), so one compiled library serves every CPU backend.
  • GPU kernels (backends/metal.py, cuda.py, tiled_gpu.py, monoidal_gpu.py): eligible ParLoops and tiled plans emit MSL or CUDA kernels. On CUDA, alpha-canonical kernel deduplication collapses structurally identical kernels across repeated layers (such as transformer blocks) into one NVRTC compile. Arrays remain device-resident across consecutive GPU kernels and across calls via par.to_device.
  • Calling convention: entry points receive flat 64-bit slots (scalars, plus pointer, offset, shape, and strides per array). Newly allocated outputs wrap into NumPy arrays without copying using a finalizer that releases the native buffer; returned input views alias caller memory directly.

Next: Design, boundaries, and history summarizes the core design principles, current compiler limits, and Parakeet's academic lineage.

docs.title: The compiled language
docs.text: Parakeet compiles a statically typed numerical subset of Python: every value has a type and array rank known at compile time. This page summarizes what is supported and where compiled code intentionally differs from CPython.

docs.title: Values and types
docs.text:
Python value Inside compiled code int, float, bool 64-bit integer, float64, bool (weakly typed like NumPy scalars) NumPy scalars (np.float32(1), np.complex64(1+2j)) Exact scalar dtype (complex lowers to unboxed (re, im) pairs) NumPy arrays bool, int8–int64, uint8–uint64, float32, float64, complex64, complex128; any rank and strides Tuples (arbitrarily nested) Compile-time structures (zero runtime overhead) NamedTuple and @dataclass (frozen or mutable) Compile-time records with pure methods, @property, __call__, and functional field rebinding (obj.x = v) Fixed string-key dict Compile-time record keyed by literal strings (key order is part of the type) Lists & comprehensions Numeric literals/comprehensions build arrays; local [] lists unbox at compile time or promote to growable CPU buffers in dynamic loops slice, range, zip, enumerate, itertools Supported as values and zero-allocation iterators (pairwise, islice, chain, product, batched) None, strings, dtypes, functions, modules Compile-time constants

Type promotion follows NumPy 2 (NEP 50) exactly: float32_arr * 2.0 stays float32, int8_arr + 1 stays int8, and int32_arr / 2 is float64.

  • float16 inputs are widened to float32.
  • complex64 / complex128 lower to unboxed (re, im) float views across CPU, Metal (complex64), and CUDA, and compose with Wirtinger par.grad and par.jvp.
  • Unsupported objects (object arrays, set, arbitrary non-dataclass class instances) raise a TypeError naming the unsupported type.

docs.title: Statements and control flow
docs.text:
Supported Not supported (UnsupportedError) Assignments (=, tuple unpack, +=, :=, annotations) try / except / finally if / elif / else, scalar match / case with context managers for (ranges, arrays, tuples, zip, enumerate), while, loop else class definitions inside @jit break, continue, early return anywhere Generators (yield) Nested def and lambda, closures global / nonlocal statements assert, raise built-in exceptions (literal message), pass, del import inside @jit, f-strings, print

Key loop and comprehension semantics:

  • Loop else runs on normal exhaustion (including empty inputs) and is skipped by break. zip(..., strict=True) checks equal lengths.
  • Chained comparisons (0 <= i < n) evaluate each reached operand once and short-circuit.
  • Cartesian comprehensions ([f(x, y) for x in xs for y in ys]) over independent ranges or arrays compile to parallel maps (rightmost iterator varies fastest) and fuse directly into scalar consumers like sum(...). Dependent inner bounds (for j in range(i)) run sequentially.

docs.title: Functions and closures
docs.text:
• All helper calls are inlined automatically—helpers do not need @par.jit. Because calls inline at compile time, recursion is not supported.
  • Positional, keyword, default, keyword-only, *args, **kwargs, **d unpacking, functools.partial, and operator.* callables all work.
  • Functions are first-class at compile time (pass them, store them, close over locals).
  • Globals and closures are read on every call, just like Python. If a global changes type, a new specialization is compiled.

docs.title: Arrays, views, and indexing
docs.text:
Compiled code matches NumPy's view and mutation semantics:

@par.jit
def f(x):
  v = x[1:]  # view of caller's array
  v[0] = 0  # mutates x in place
  x += 1  # visible to caller
  y = x * 2  # newly allocated array
  x[1:] = x[:-1]  # overlapping slice assignment is safe
  return y
  • Basic slicing (x[i, 1:-1, ::2, None, ...]), integer-array indexing, and boolean masks work for both reads and writes.
  • Returning an input returns the same object; returning a view returns a NumPy view over caller memory. Writing to a read-only array raises ValueError.
  • Indices are bounds-checked (IndexError) and broadcast shapes are checked (ValueError). Pass @par.jit(bounds_check=False) once code is verified.

docs.title: Lists and dynamic loops
docs.text:
• Numeric list literals ([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) and comprehensions build NumPy arrays directly.
  • Local scratch lists (outs = []; outs.append(...)) stay unboxed at compile time in straight-line or unrolled code (so np.stack(outs) and RaggedArray.from_sequences(outs) allocate zero Python objects and compose with par.grad), and automatically promote to a growable CPU buffer when mutated inside a runtime loop or dynamic branch.
  • Parallel & GPU scratch: inside par.parfor / par.map bodies and GPU kernels, use par.fixed_list(capacity, dtype) for a stack-allocated, zero-malloc buffer.
  • Shape rebinding: variables holding arrays or RaggedArrays can be rebound to new shapes across for / while iterations (for example active = active[mask]).

docs.title: Dataclasses and fixed records
docs.text:
NamedTuples, @dataclasses (frozen or non-frozen), and fixed string-key dicts can cross the @par.jit boundary and hold arrays, scalars, static metadata, or nested records.

  • Pure methods, @property, @staticmethod, @classmethod, and __call__ inline at compile time with zero PyObject overhead.
  • Local field updates (obj.x = v, obj.x += v) on non-frozen dataclasses functionally rebind the compile-time record (value semantics, no heap mutation).
  • Returning a record reconstructs its Python type while preserving NumPy view semantics for array fields.

docs.title: Differences from CPython / NumPy
docs.text: Topic Behavior in Parakeet One static type per variable Merging int and float across branches promotes both paths to float. Incompatible types (e.g. array and None) fail at compile time if used afterward. Static array rank Every array's ndim is fixed at compile time. Operations with value-dependent output rank (such as np.squeeze(x) without axis=) require an explicit axis=. Compile-time constants Arguments like axis, keepdims, dtype, and shape tuple length must be static. When passed as function arguments, Parakeet specializes on their values automatically. 64-bit integer overflow Python ints compile to 64-bit signed integers that wrap on overflow (like NumPy int64), not arbitrary-precision bigints. Unentered loop variables A variable first assigned inside a loop keeps its final value after the loop, or 0 if the loop ran zero times (CPython raises NameError). Random number streams np.random uses Parakeet's parallel RNG (par.seed); values are statistically valid but differ from NumPy's stream. Parallel evaluation order Array expressions, comprehensions, and par.map run elements in parallel in unspecified order. User reductions run in parallel only when associativity is proved (+, *, min, max, &, |, ^); otherwise left-to-right.

docs.title: Migrating from Parakeet 0.x
docs.text:
Parakeet 1.x is a rewrite for Python 3.11+. The decorator and the operators keep their names, and most 0.x programs run after the usual Python 2 → 3 changes (xrange → range, / → // for integer division, print(...)).

0.x 1.x Python 2.7, dsltools, appdirs Python 3.11+, NumPy 2, nothing else config.backend = "openmp" still works; default is "auto", which needs no OpenMP "llvm" backend removed "interp" backend "python" (runs the original function) "cuda" via PyCUDA + nvcc "cuda" via CuPy, no toolkit install; new "metal" backend f(x, _backend="c") unchanged; also @jit(backend="c") @macro still there, with a different contract: the function gets the compiler and the compile-time values of its arguments instead of syntax nodes (this is how map, reduce and the NumPy functions are defined). @typed_macro and @staged_macro are gone; arguments such as axis are specialised automatically parakeet.testing_helpers parakeet.testing (the old name still imports) config.opt_fusion, config.print_specialized_function, config.print_generated_code still accepted, as aliases of fusion, print_ir and print_code; the other opt_* flags are gone (see Configuration) parakeet.prims.add, parakeet.ndtypes.Int64, Float64, ... unchanged tuple parameters def f((a, b)) not valid Python 3; unpack in the body typed_repr(f, args), specialize(f, args), run_python_fn(f, args) unchanged (also f.specialize(*args).ir) find_broken_transform(fn, inputs, expected) unchanged in spirit: it switches fusion, tiling, the C optimizer and parallel loops on one at a time and names the first that changes the result parakeet.frontend, parakeet.syntax, parakeet.transforms, parakeet.lib the same packages, with new contents: the staged interpreter, the loop IR, and tiling / differentiation parakeet.rank, size, shape, erf, norm, ... unchanged

docs.title: Behaviour changes
docs.text:
• Result types follow NumPy 2. In 0.x bool + bool gave an integer and integer power gave a float; now both give what NumPy gives. Python scalars no longer upcast float32 arrays.
  • Bounds are checked by default. Programs that silently read out of bounds under 0.x now raise IndexError.
  • np.array(x) copies, x += 1 updates in place, views alias: as in NumPy.
  • Globals are read at call time rather than captured at first compilation.
  • parakeet.reduce is parallel only for combiners known to be associative; 0.x assumed associativity for any function.
  • imap(f, shape) passes f a tuple whenever shape is a tuple, including one-element tuples.

docs.title: Data-parallel operators
docs.text:
Parakeet exposes one unified set of data-parallel operators on the top-level parakeet module. Every operator works both inside @par.jit (fusing with surrounding NumPy code) and directly from ordinary Python (automatically compiling callable arguments):

import numpy as np
import parakeet as par

docs.title: Choosing an operator
docs.text:
Goal Operator(s) Transform slices or elements in parallel par.map, par.imap Pairwise or Cartesian-product operations par.allpairs, par.outer_map Reduce an array or index grid par.reduce, par.ireduce, par.fold Running prefix sum or recurrence par.scan Boolean compaction or 1-to-K ragged expansion par.filter, par.filter_reduce, par.flatmap, par.filter_pairs Histograms and indexed accumulation par.scatter_add 2D / banded dynamic programming par.wavefront, par.batched_wavefront, par.soft_align Side-effecting parallel loops par.parfor

For differentiation (par.grad, par.jvp, par.hvp), see Automatic differentiation. To see how all of these operators indexify onto Parakeet's internal operator core (and how fusion and tiling fire on them), see Operators & compilation walkthrough.

docs.title: par.map(f, *args, axis=0)
docs.text:
Apply f in parallel to corresponding slices along axis (or to every scalar element with broadcasting when axis=None). Non-array arguments are passed unchanged, and f may return a scalar, tuple, or array (results are stacked).

par.map(lambda row: row / np.sum(row), X)  # normalize each row
par.map(lambda a, b: a * a + b, x, y, axis=None)  # element-wise with broadcast

docs.title: par.imap(f, shape)
docs.text:
Build an array of shape where entry (i, j, ...) is f(i, j, ...). Multi-axis indices unpack automatically when f takes len(shape) arguments (a 1-arg tuple lambda ij: also works).

par.imap(lambda i, j: i >= j, (T, T))  # causal mask (fuses with zero allocation)

docs.title: par.allpairs(f, x, y, axis=0)
docs.text:
Evaluate f(x[i], y[j]) for every pair of slices (i, j) along axis. Fuses directly into downstream reductions like par.fold or np.argmin without materializing the N × M matrix.

par.allpairs(lambda a, b: np.sum((a - b) ** np.float32(2)), X, C)

docs.title: par.outer_map(f, *args)
docs.text: N-ary generalization of par.allpairs over the Cartesian product of the leading axes of two or more arrays.

docs.title: par.parfor(f, shape)
docs.text: Run f(i, ...) in parallel across shape for its side effects (such as writing disjoint slices or using thread-local par.fixed_list scratch). For pure array outputs, prefer NumPy expressions, comprehensions, par.map, or par.imap.

docs.title: par.reduce(f, *args, init=None, axis=None, map=None)
docs.text:
Reduce elements with binary combiner f (such as np.add, np.maximum, or a custom function), globally (axis=None) or along axis. Passing map=g fuses a map step directly into the reduction.

par.reduce(np.maximum, X, axis=0)  # column maxima
par.reduce(np.add, x, y, map=np.multiply)  # dot product, zero temporaries

docs.title: par.ireduce(f, shape, init=None, combine=np.add)
docs.text:
Reduce f(i, ...) directly over every coordinate of shape using combine, without constructing an input array first.

par.ireduce(lambda r: a[i, r] + b[r, j], k, combine=np.minimum)

docs.title: par.fold(lift, merge, x, init=None, *, axis=None, indexed=False, emit=None)
docs.text:
Associative structured reduction over multi-field tuple or NamedTuple states:

  • lift maps each element (or (value, index) when indexed=True) to a state of scalar fields.
  • merge(left, right) combines two adjacent states in input order (preserving exact left-to-right tie and NaN semantics).
  • emit optionally projects the final state.
  • init seeds the fold and is returned for empty input (without init, an empty lane raises ValueError).
# Exact argmin carrying (best_dist, best_idx) with first-index tie breaking
par.fold(
  lambda v, i: (v, i),
  lambda a, b: a if a[0] <= b[0] else b,
  scores,
  axis=1,
  indexed=True,
  emit=lambda state: state[1],
)

When composed with par.allpairs (or broadcasting NumPy np.argmin(np.sum((x[:, None] - y[None, :]) ** 2, axis=2), axis=1)), Parakeet automatically compiles a tiled pairwise fold on both CPU and GPU without allocating the Q × R score matrix.

docs.title: par.scan(f, *args, init=None, axis=0, map=None, emit=None)
docs.text:
Running prefix fold along axis (a generalization of np.cumsum and np.cumprod). Associative combiners compile to a 3-stage parallel prefix scan, and affine/bilinear recurrences trigger Law 4 chunkwise duality.

par.scan(np.add, x, y, map=lambda a, b: a - b)  # running sum of differences
par.scan(lambda acc, v: 0.9 * acc + 0.1 * v, x)  # exponential moving average

docs.title: par.filter(pred, *args, map=None)
docs.text:
Return elements where pred holds (optionally transforming kept elements with map). Equivalent to NumPy boolean masking x[pred(x)].

par.filter(lambda a, b: a > b, x, y, map=np.add)  # x + y where x > y

docs.title: par.filter_reduce(f, pred, *args, map=None, init=None, axis=None)
docs.text: Reduce with f over elements satisfying pred. When init is provided, fuses into a single zero-allocation guarded reduction loop (also triggered automatically by np.sum(x[x > 0])).

docs.title: par.flatmap(count_fn, emit_fn, *xs)
docs.text:
Two-pass 1-to-K ragged expansion returning a RaggedArray(values, offsets). For each index i, count_fn(x0[i], ...) returns the output count c_i >= 0, and emit_fn(x0[i], ..., k) emits item k (0 <= k < c_i) in parallel after a prefix sum of counts.

# Expand run-length-encoded CIGAR operations into a RaggedArray
par.flatmap(lambda op, n: n, lambda op, n, k: op, ops, lengths)

docs.title: par.filter_pairs(pred, x, y, emit=None)
docs.text: Compact all pairs (i, j) where pred(x[i], y[j]) holds into a RaggedArray of matching pairs (or emit(x[i], y[j]) payloads) without allocating a dense N × M mask.

docs.title: par.scatter_add(n, idx, vals, where=None)
docs.text:
Accumulate vals[i] into output bin idx[i] of length n (optionally guarded by where, or passed as a keyed generator ((k, v) for ...)). Compiles with thread-privatized histograms on CPU, parallel atomics on GPU, sibling fusion for shared idx, and an exact gather adjoint under par.grad. Also triggered automatically by np.bincount, np.add.at, and canonical out[idx[i]] += v loops.

grad_hist = par.scatter_add(256, bin_ids, grads)

docs.title: par.wavefront(step_fn, shape, init_top, init_left, *, init_corner=None, band=None, track_max=False)
docs.text: Execute a 2D or diagonally banded dynamic programming recurrence along parallel anti-diagonals in O(M) rolling memory (never allocating the full M × N table). step_fn(top, left, diag, i, j) returns the next scalar or tuple/NamedTuple state (e.g. 3-state affine-gap alignment).

docs.title: par.batched_wavefront(...)
docs.text: Run par.wavefront independently across a batch of sequences or grids in parallel (one thread/lane per batch item on CPU or GPU).

docs.title: par.soft_align(scores, gamma=1.0, gap=-1.0, band=None)
docs.text: Differentiable soft-maximum global or banded sequence alignment with a checkpointed reverse-mode VJP under par.grad / par.value_and_grad.

docs.title: Specialized data & scratch helpers
docs.text:
For ragged workloads, byte parsing, and per-thread scratch inside parallel loops:

Helper Purpose par.fixed_list(capacity, dtype=np.float32) Stack-allocated, zero-malloc scratch list (.append, .pop, .clear, indexing, len) for CPU, CUDA, and Metal parallel bodies par.split_bytes(buf, sep=10, skip_empty=False) / par.parse_int64 / par.parse_float32 / par.parse_float64 Zero-PyObject delimiter splitting into RaggedArray[uint8] and compiled ASCII numeric parsing par.partition_by_size / par.segmented_parfor / par.segmented_histogram2d / par.ragged_partition Adaptive 3-tier ragged dispatch (heavy/medium/light tiers), fused 2D (grad, hess, count) histograms, and parallel CSR partitioning

docs.title: Semantics notes
docs.text:
• Array-returning functions: par.map may return arrays (stacked along the mapped axis). All outputs must share the same shape (ValueError at runtime if ragged).
  • Associativity & parallelism: par.reduce runs in parallel only when its combiner is recognizably one of +, *, min, max, and, or, &, |, ^ (written as np.add, lambda a, b: a + b, or par.add). Non-associative combiners run sequentially left-to-right like functools.reduce. Floating-point parallel reductions may differ in the last ULP, like NumPy's pairwise summation.
  • Combiners: Standard NumPy ufuncs (np.add, np.multiply, np.minimum, np.maximum) are idiomatic; par.add / parakeet.dsl aliases remain available for compatibility.

docs.title: Performance and tuning
docs.text:
Cross-library benchmarks

For head-to-head comparisons against PyTorch, torch.compile, JAX, CuPy, Faiss, PyKeOps, RDKit, Biopython, and edlib on NVIDIA L4 and Apple M1 Pro, see Benchmarks. This page explains when Parakeet wins or loses and how to tune your code.

docs.title: Where Parakeet wins vs. where it doesn't
docs.text: Parakeet excels at Specialist libraries still lead on Multi-step array expressions (eliminates temporaries, single pass over RAM) Large standalone GPU GEMMs (use cuBLAS; on CPU, Parakeet already calls NumPy's BLAS) Pairwise kernels, attention, cross-entropy, 1-NN (O(N²) buffers tiled away) Single-threaded transcendentals (np.tanh, np.exp — NumPy uses SIMD; Parakeet wins once multi-core kicks in) Algorithms that would otherwise need a Python loop (stencils, Julia set, DP, bit-parallel bio kernels) Tiny inputs (~10–100 elements), where native call marshalling outweighs work Multi-core CPU scaling & GIL-free concurrency Memory-bound GPU loops that copy host arrays back and forth on every call (use par.to_device)

docs.title: CPU micro-benchmarks (Apple M1 Pro, 10 cores, float64)
docs.text:
Measured via python benchmarks/run.py (best of 5, compilation excluded; × is speedup over NumPy):

Benchmark NumPy backend="c" (1T) backend="multicore" (10T) np.tanh(x * a) + b (4M) 14.5 ms 24.8 ms (0.6×) 3.5 ms (4.2×) Euclidean norm (4M) 3.4 ms 1.1 ms (3.1×) 0.65 ms (5.3×) Arc distance (4M) 174 ms 174 ms (1.0×) 23.3 ms (7.5×) Rosenbrock derivative (4M) 11.4 ms 8.7 ms (1.3×) 0.72 ms (16×) Harris corner response (2000²) 19.4 ms 4.0 ms (4.9×) 1.1 ms (17×) Diffusion stencil, 20 steps (1000²) 54.5 ms 24.5 ms (2.2×) 6.3 ms (8.6×) All-pairs distances (40k × 64 × 32) 103 ms 11.1 ms (9.2×) 1.6 ms (66×) 3×3 convolution (2000²) 21.2 ms 9.1 ms (2.3×) 1.4 ms (15×) Julia set (1000²) 402 ms 47.2 ms (8.5×) 6.1 ms (66×) Matrix product (300², blas=False) 0.16 ms 4.1 ms 0.72 ms

docs.title: Compute-bound vs. transfer-bound on GPUs
docs.text:
GPUs win decisively when arithmetic intensity is high (many FLOPs per byte loaded) or when arrays stay resident across iterations via par.to_device. Measured with python benchmarks/gpu_showcase.py on an NVIDIA A100 (12 CPU threads, float32, identical Python source):

Kernel Size NumPy 1 core 12 threads A100 A100 vs 12T N-body forces 16,384 bodies – 1,393 ms 238 ms 7.5 ms 32× K-means assignment 2M × 256 × 16 2,247 ms 9,551 ms 1,913 ms 75.8 ms 25× Heat equation, 200 steps 2048² 7,821 ms 4,532 ms 370 ms 118 ms 3.1× Black-Scholes 20M options 625 ms 1,746 ms 227 ms 111 ms 2.0× Julia set 4096² – 1,425 ms 155 ms 95.5 ms 1.6×

N-body and k-means do thousands of operations per output element (186× faster than 1 core on n-body). Heat equation runs 600 kernels on device-resident grids with zero intermediate host copies (down from 1.4 s before residency). Black-Scholes is mostly PCIe transfer (240 MB in, 80 MB out)—passing par.to_device inputs removes that bus bottleneck across repeated calls.

docs.title: Cache and register tiling
docs.text:
Any 2D+ map wrapping a reduction (a @ b, allpairs, einsum, tropical products) sweeps through the second operand on every row if run naively, thrashing L1/L2 cache. Parakeet automatically tiles the inner dimension to fit config.tile_bytes (default half of per-core L2) and jams 2×4 register micro-tiles on CPU (and shared-memory + matrix-unit tiles on GPU).

a @ b on 1024 × 1024 float64 (Apple M1 Max, config.blas = False):

Schedule 1 core All cores Untiled (tiling=False) 190 ms 43 ms Tiled (default) 92 ms 13 ms NumPy (Accelerate BLAS, blas=True) — 4.5 ms

Disable tiling with @par.jit(tiling=False) or par.config.tiling = False. On CPU, standalone float a @ b calls NumPy's BLAS directly by default (config.blas = True).

docs.title: Practical tuning checklist
docs.text:
• Keep arrays contiguous: specializations track C-contiguity; unit-stride arrays vectorize cleanly on CPU and coalesce on GPU.
  • Keep GPU arrays resident: wrap repeated GPU inputs with par.to_device so you do not pay host-to-device transfers on every call.
  • Use float32 on Apple Metal: Metal has no hardware float64 and falls back to CPU for double-precision loops.
  • Enable Tensor Cores on NVIDIA sm_80+: set par.config.tensor_cores = True (or PARAKEET_TENSOR_CORES=1) for TF32 WMMA matmuls and training steps.
  • Prefer expressions / operators over raw for loops: NumPy expressions, comprehensions, par.map, par.fold, and par.scatter_add parallelize automatically; arbitrary sequential for loops do not (except recognized Law 4 affine/bilinear recurrences and canonical out[idx[i]] += v scatters).
  • Inline across helpers: put the outer workflow inside one @par.jit function so fusion crosses helper boundaries automatically.
  • Drop checks when verified: @par.jit(bounds_check=False) eliminates bounds checks in tight indexed loops; par.config.fast_math = True enables -ffast-math when exact IEEE rounding is not required.

docs.title: Why Parakeet is built this way
docs.text:
Numerical Python sits between two worlds. NumPy gives concise, readable code and fast C/Fortran kernels for individual operations, but composing expressions allocates temporary arrays and sweeps DRAM on every step—and any algorithm that does not fit a built-in ufunc falls back to slow CPython loops. C/CUDA compilers generate fast scalar loops, but once array code is flattened into imperative for-loops, high-level structure (independence, associativity, data reuse) is lost and must be painfully recovered by dependence analysis.

Parakeet—originating in the NYU theses of Eric Hielscher (2013) and Alex Rubinsteyn (2014) and HotPar '12—bridges that gap with one guiding idea: keep array programs in algebraic operator form (data-parallel adverbs over explicit index spaces) all the way through optimization. That single choice unifies five design principles:

  1. Specialize on types, values, and shape buckets at call time. Python functions act as templates specialized on argument dtypes, array ranks, layouts, and container structure. Compile-time parameters (axis=, tuple length, size-1 broadcast dimensions) specialize automatically, and tiled GPU schedules propagate power-of-2 shape buckets and divisibility so aligned sizes share one branchless binary.
  2. Normalize everything into coordinate-driven primitives. NumPy expressions, comprehensions, matrix products, einsum, and par.* calls all indexify into six source primitives (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter/IndexExpand, IndexScatter, IndexWavefront), turning broadcasts, transposes, and slices into plain index arithmetic (Operators & compilation walkthrough).
  3. Fuse algebraically before lowering to loops. Vertical, nested, filter, sibling, and online fusion operate directly on the operator IR with explicit alias, single-use cost, and associativity guards (Rewrite rules catalog).
  4. Tile for cache and GPU shared memory from one IR. Following Hielscher's locality framework, target-aware reduction interchange, IndexTile cache/register blocking, GPU SRAM staging, hardware matrix units (Metal simdgroup_matrix, CUDA TF32 WMMA), and Laws 1–6 all run on the same operator IR before codegen.
  5. Inspectable, fail-loud compilation. Unsupported constructs raise a source-located CompileError instead of silently falling back; every pass is verified by par.verify and inspectable via par.show_rewrite, f.specialize(), and par.find_broken_transform.

docs.title: NumPy, SciPy, AD, and GPUs
docs.text:
• NumPy & SciPy: ~215 NumPy functions and ufuncs are built in (full list), including einsum, np.unique, np.searchsorted, 2D & batched 3D np.linalg (cholesky, det, solve, inv, qr, eigh, eigvalsh, svd, pinv, lstsq, norm), and parallel np.random. Not built in: non-symmetric eig/eigvals, 4D+ np.linalg (wrap with par.map), np.fft.* (see examples/complex_fft_and_fasta.py for a compiled radix-2 FFT), np.lexsort/np.isin, and scipy.*.
  • Automatic differentiation: covers reverse mode (grad, vjp, jacrev), forward mode (jvp, linearize, jacfwd), linear_transpose, higher-order AD (hvp, hessian), checkpointed for/while loops, and Law 2 rematerialization. Refused loudly: break/continue over differentiated state, runtime if branches with array stores or control exits, cumprod, convolve, arbitrary indexed overwrites (out[idx] = v), overwriting a buffer needed by an earlier VJP, and reverse-over-reverse through non-scalar par.map bodies.
  • GPUs & locality: Apple Metal lacks hardware float64 (falls back to CPU with a warning); parallel bodies that dynamically allocate arrays per thread run on CPU; standalone GPU GEMMs use Parakeet's tiled kernels (fusing prologues/epilogues, though trailing cuBLAS on large standalone matmuls); tile sizes are chosen analytically from TargetProfile rather than online search; chunkwise TileScan covers affine and bilinear recurrences rather than arbitrary scans.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
Parakeet began in OCaml as an array compiler modeling the array language Q, shifted to modeling Python, and was reimplemented in Python at New York University (Courant Institute) by co-creators Alex Rubinsteyn (@iskandr) and Eric Hielscher (@hielscher), with Nathaniel Weinman, advised by Dennis Shasha, and with early advice from Russell Power (@rjpower). That earlier system was hosted at parakeetpython.com and documented in:

  • Eric Hielscher, Locality Optimization for Data Parallel Programs (PhD thesis, NYU, 2013; also NYU TR2013-955 / arXiv:1304.1835 with Alex Rubinsteyn and Dennis Shasha): TiledMap, TiledReduce, and TiledScan for cache tiling, register blocking, and loop interchange over adverb trees.
  • Alex Rubinsteyn, Runtime Compilation of Array-Oriented Python Programs (PhD thesis, NYU, 2014): type and value specialization, data-parallel adverbs, and algebraic fusion.
  • Papers and talks: HotPar '12 (Parakeet: A Just-In-Time Parallel Accelerator for Python, with Alex Rubinsteyn, Eric Hielscher, Nathaniel Weinman, and Dennis Shasha), PyData Boston '13, and PyData NYC '13 (Python on the GPU with Parakeet).

Parakeet 1.x is a ground-up rewrite for Python 3.11+ and NumPy 2 that keeps @jit NumPy and explicit data-parallel operators together, closes the soundness gaps from the earlier design, and adds Apple Metal, NVIDIA CUDA, composable AD, and tiled monoidal reductions.

docs.title: Why compile through an operator algebra?
docs.text:
NumPy is fast on any single operation because each call drops into compiled C or Fortran. The bottleneck shows up when you compose operations:

  • Streaming expressions allocate and re-read memory. A one-line formula like np.tanh(x * a) + b makes three sweeps over RAM and allocates two temporary arrays. A four-line attention function allocates three O(T²) matrices.
  • Custom algorithms fall back to Python. Anything that does not fit a single NumPy ufunc (pairwise distances, custom folds, banded DP, tree splits) either explodes memory with broadcasting or drops into a slow CPython loop.

Traditional compilers lower array code straight into nested C for-loops and then try to re-discover parallelism, associativity, and cache reuse through fragile loop-nest dependence analysis. Following the NYU Parakeet theses (Rubinsteyn 2014, Hielscher 2013), Parakeet does the opposite: it keeps array programs in algebraic operator form until the final lowering step. Because independence, associativity, and data reuse stay explicit in the IR, fusion, cache/GPU tiling, and differentiation become small, sound algebraic rewrites.

docs.title: What does the Index prefix mean?
docs.text:
In compiler output (par.show_rewrite, spec.operators), internal primitives carry an Index prefix: IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, IndexExpand, IndexScatter, IndexWavefront, and IndexTile.

Why not just Map and Reduce?

At the Python surface, operators are array-driven: par.map(f, X) iterates over elements of X, par.allpairs(f, X, Y) takes pairs of slices, X[:, None] - Y[None, :] broadcasts shapes, X.T permutes axes, and X[::2] strides. If the optimizer worked directly on array-driven nodes, it would need separate fusion and tiling rules for every combination (Map ∘ Transpose, Reduce ∘ Broadcast, Reduce ∘ AllPairs, Map ∘ Slice, …).

Instead, elaboration indexifies every array expression into a coordinate-driven operator:

  • An Index* node takes no input arrays of its own—only a rectangular integer coordinate box shape = (N₀, N₁, …) and a body parameterized by integer coordinates (i, j, …) that explicitly indexes whatever arrays it needs (A[i, k], B[k, j]).
  • Broadcasting, transposes, slices, views, comprehensions, and allpairs vanish into simple index expressions before any middle-end pass runs.

That single normalization is why one fusion pass (IndexMap into IndexReduce) automatically handles np.sum(x * x), np.sum(x.T[::2]), a @ b.T, np.einsum('ij,jk->ik', a, b), and np.argmin(np.sum((x[:, None] - y[None, :])**2, axis=2), axis=1) without a single special case for broadcasting or transposes.

docs.title: From Python and par.* to the seven primitives
docs.text:
Everything you write in NumPy, Python, or par.* lowers into six source primitives, and the locality optimizer adds a seventh (IndexTile) when blocking reductions for CPU cache or GPU shared memory:

Internal primitive Surface NumPy / Python idioms par.* operators that reduce here What it captures IndexMap Element-wise ufuncs, broadcasting, slices/views materialized, np.where, comprehensions, @ / einsum outer grid par.map, par.each, par.imap, par.allpairs, par.outer_map, par.parfor, par.pmap1/pmap2 Independent work at every coordinate (i, j, …) IndexReduce np.sum, prod, min, max, mean, var, std, all, any, argmin, argmax, inner dot of @ / einsum par.reduce, par.ireduce, par.fold, par.topk_fold Associative reduction or ordered multi-field (Carry) fold IndexScan np.cumsum, np.cumprod, affine/bilinear for t in range(T): loops par.scan Running prefix accumulation where step t depends on 0..t IndexFilter Boolean masking x[mask], np.nonzero, np.flatnonzero par.filter, par.filter_reduce (with IndexReduce), par.split_bytes 1-to-0/1 stream compaction by predicate IndexExpand Variable-length emission into RaggedArray par.flatmap, par.filter_pairs Two-pass 1-to-K ragged compaction (count → prefix sum → emit) IndexScatter np.bincount, np.add.at, canonical for i: out[idx[i]] += v, inverted [np.sum(v[idx == b]) for b in range(n)] par.scatter_add, par.segmented_histogram2d Associative accumulation into shared output bins IndexWavefront Anti-diagonal and banded 2D DP recurrences par.wavefront, par.batched_wavefront, par.soft_align Cell (i, j) depends on (i−1, j), (i, j−1), (i−1, j−1) IndexTile (optimizer-emitted) Emitted automatically from IndexMap wrapping IndexReduce (@, einsum, 1-NN, attention, RBF) (Never written directly) Blocked execution with staged L1/L2 cache, register, or GPU SRAM tiles

docs.title: Map (IndexMap)
docs.text: Evaluates a pure body independently at every coordinate of an N-D box. Because iterations are independent, vertical chains collapse (np.tanh(x * a) + b), sibling maps merge (sin(x), cos(x)), and nested maps flatten into one multi-dimensional grid for CPU threads and GPUs.

docs.title: Reduce and Fold (IndexReduce)
docs.text: Combines values across a reduction box into one or more scalar accumulators. Associative combiners (+, *, min, max, bitwise ops) split across threads and SIMD lanes. Structured state—like (best_val, best_idx) in argmin or Welford variance in par.fold—attaches as Carry fields that merge in strict left-to-right order so ties and NaNs stay exact.

docs.title: Scan (IndexScan)
docs.text: Computes running prefixes (np.cumsum, par.scan) via a 3-stage parallel chunk scan. Consumer maps fuse directly into the scan's emit block (np.cumsum(x) * 2 + 1 in one pass), and plain Python affine/bilinear for loops rewrite via Law 4 chunkwise duality.

docs.title: Filter and Expand (IndexFilter, IndexExpand)
docs.text: Compacts sparse or variable-length outputs without serial locks. Chained filters merge (x[p][q] → p and q), and IndexFilter followed by IndexReduce collapses into a zero-allocation guarded loop (np.sum(x[x > 0])).

docs.title: Scatter (IndexScatter)
docs.text: Accumulates associatively into indexed bins. Sibling histograms sharing an index array merge into a single pass, lower to thread-privatized bins on CPU and atomics on GPU, and differentiate to a gather (g[idx]) under par.grad.

docs.title: Wavefront (IndexWavefront)
docs.text: Schedules 2D dynamic programming along parallel anti-diagonals in O(M) rolling memory, never allocating the full M × N DP table.

docs.title: Tile (IndexTile)
docs.text: Following Hielscher (2013), middle-end locality passes rewrite IndexMap wrapping IndexReduce into nested IndexTile operators with explicit TileStage buffers—driving CPU L1/L2 cache blocking, 2×4 register jamming, GPU __shared__ / threadgroup memory, Metal simdgroup_matrix, and CUDA TF32 WMMA from one representation.

docs.title: Worked compilation walkthroughs
docs.text: Each walkthrough below starts from ordinary Python/NumPy and shows the exact compiled schedule Parakeet produces. (To inspect raw SSA loop IR, see Compiler architecture: Lowered IR.)

docs.title: 1. Causal self-attention (O(T²) NumPy → O(T) tiled kernel)
docs.text:
Start from four lines of ordinary NumPy:

@par.jit
def causal_attention(q, k, v):
  causal = par.imap(lambda i, j: i >= j, (q.shape[0], k.shape[0]))
  s = np.where(causal, (q @ k.T) * np.float32(0.125), np.float32(-1e9))
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ v

Three general passes transform this function:

  1. Indexification & delayed fusion fold causal, * 0.125, and np.where directly into Q @ K.T (so no T × T boolean mask is ever allocated), leaving three O(T²) float buffers (scores, exp_s, weights).
  2. normalize hoists row_max and row_sum out of the column loop so each row reduction runs once instead of T times.
  3. monoidal tiling (Law 1 + Law 5) recognizes the softmax-weighted contraction as an associative rescaled monoid (m, l, o) and drops all three O(T²) buffers. TileInterval (Law 5) proves upper-triangular tiles (j0 > i0 + BM - 1) are fully masked and skips loading them, while interior tiles run branchless.
Naive execution 4 passes · 3 × O(T²) buffers 
scores = np.empty((T, T), np.float32)
for i in range(T):
  for j in range(T):
    dot = sum(q[i, d] * k[j, d] for d in range(D))
    scores[i, j] = dot * 0.125 if i >= j else -1e9

exp_s = np.empty((T, T), np.float32)
for i in range(T):
  row_max = max(scores[i, :])
  exp_s[i, :] = np.exp(scores[i, :] - row_max)

weights = exp_s / np.sum(exp_s, axis=1, keepdims=True)
out = weights @ v
Compiled schedule (Law 1 + Law 5) 1 pass · 0 O(T²) buffers 
out = np.empty((T, D), np.float32)
for i0 in parallel_range(0, T, BM):
  Q_tile = stage(q[i0 : i0 + BM])
  m, l, o = fill(-inf), fill(0.0), zeros((BM, D))

  for j0 in range(0, T, BN):
    if j0 > i0 + BM - 1:  # Law 5: skip upper triangle
      continue
    K_tile = stage(k[j0 : j0 + BN])
    V_tile = stage(v[j0 : j0 + BN])
    full = j0 + BN - 1 <= i0  # interior -> branchless
    m, l, o = monoid_step(m, l, o, Q_tile, K_tile, V_tile, full)

  out[i0 : i0 + BM] = o / l[:, None]

Verify what fired with par.show_rewrite(causal_attention, q, k, v).summary():

Parakeet Algebraic Rewrite Report for `causal_attention`
  Laws triggered : Law 1: Rescaled Semiring Monoid Tile Fusion, Law 5: Affine Tile-Interval Mask Pruning
  Monoidal plans : flash_monoid
  Operators      : IndexMap 5 -> 1 | IndexTile 1 | IndexScatter 0 -> 0 | Carry folds 0

docs.title: 2. Exact 1-NN (broadcasting NumPy → tiled pairwise fold)
docs.text:
@par.jit
def nearest(x, y):
  delta = x[:, None, :] - y[None, :, :]
  d2 = np.sum(delta ** np.float32(2), axis=2)
  return np.argmin(d2, axis=1)

Indexification turns the 3D broadcast delta and squared sum d2 directly into index expressions inside argmin—eliminating both the (Q, R, D) difference tensor and (Q, R) distance matrix. Law 6 (pairwise fold tiling) then blocks the search into 16 × 128 L1/SRAM score tiles merged strictly left-to-right so ties and NaNs keep NumPy's exact first-index rule:

Naive NumPy O(Q · R · D) + O(Q · R) RAM 
delta = x[:, None, :] - y[None, :, :]  # (Q, R, D)
d2 = np.sum(delta**2, axis=2)  # (Q, R): 64 MiB
out = np.argmin(d2, axis=1)  # (Q,)
Parakeet Tiled Fold 8 KiB L1 / 16 KiB SRAM 
out = np.empty(Q, np.int64)
for q0 in parallel_range(0, Q, 16):
  best_d, best_j = fill(+inf), zeros(16, np.int64)
  for r0 in range(0, R, 128):  # ordered in r0
    tile = microtile_2x4(x[q0 : q0 + 16], y[r0 : r0 + 128])
    best_d, best_j = merge_ordered(best_d, best_j, tile, r0)
  out[q0 : q0 + 16] = best_j

On CUDA and Metal, the same pass emits a 2-stage schedule: Stage 1 computes 16 KiB shared-memory tiles and writes O(Q · #tiles) partial winners; Stage 2 merges partial winners in global reference order.

docs.title: 3. Boolean masking → zero-allocation FilterReduce
docs.text:
@par.jit
def pos_sum(x):
  return np.sum(x[x > 0.0])

Because the compacted index array has no other consumer and add has identity 0.0, filter fusion collapses IndexFilter + IndexReduce into a single guarded parallel reduction with zero allocation and no gather bounds check:

Before filter fusion 2 passes · index alloc 
kept = [i for i in range(N) if x[i] > 0.0]
total = sum(x[i] for i in kept)
After filter fusion 1 pass · 0 allocations 
partials = parallel_chunks(N)
for chunk in partials:
  acc = 0.0
  for i in chunk:
    if x[i] > 0.0:
      acc += x[i]
total = sum(partials)

docs.text:

# 1. Summary of algebraic laws triggered and operator counts

# 2. Generated C and GPU kernel source

docs.title: Requirements and install
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+ and NumPy 2
  • A system C compiler: Xcode command line tools on macOS (xcode-select --install), gcc or clang on Linux, MinGW-w64 or LLVM on Windows
pip install parakeet
python -c "import parakeet; print(parakeet.available_backends())"

available_backends() reports "ok" for each usable backend or explains what is missing and how to install it. For GPUs, install parakeet[metal] on Apple Silicon or parakeet[cuda12] with an NVIDIA GPU.

docs.title: Your first compiled function
docs.text:
Decorate any numerical function with @par.jit:

import numpy as np
import parakeet as par


@par.jit
def rms(x):
  return np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x))


x = np.random.rand(1_000_000)
rms(x)  # first call: compiles for (float64, 1-d), then runs
rms(x)  # later calls: straight into cached native code
rms(x.astype(np.float32))  # compiles a separate float32 specialization

Compilation takes a few hundred milliseconds per specialization (mostly in the C compiler) and is cached on disk across runs. par.jit also wraps lambdas or plain functions directly, and par.run(fn, *args) compiles and calls in one step:

fast_rms = par.jit(lambda x: np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x)))
par.run(rms.fn, x)

docs.title: Loops, comprehensions, and helpers
docs.text:
Anything in the compiled language mixes freely. Helper functions are inlined automatically—they do not need @par.jit:

def sqr_dist(a, b):
  return np.sum((a - b) ** 2)


@par.jit
def nearest(X, centroids):
  return np.array([np.argmin([sqr_dist(x, c) for c in centroids]) for x in X])

When you want explicit data-parallel control over slices, pairs, scans, or histograms, use par.map, par.reduce, par.fold, par.scan, par.allpairs, or par.scatter_add.

docs.title: Gradients in one line
docs.text:
Wrap any scalar-valued function with par.grad or par.value_and_grad. The forward and backward passes compile together into one native function:

def mse_loss(w, x, y):
  return np.mean((np.tanh(x @ w) - y) ** 2)


loss_val, dw = par.value_and_grad(mse_loss)(w, x, y)

See Automatic differentiation for nested tuples, @dataclass parameters, par.jvp, par.hvp, and custom rules.

docs.title: Picking a backend
docs.text:
By default (backend="auto"), Parakeet parallelizes across all CPU cores. Switch backends per function, per call, globally, or for a block:

@par.jit(backend="metal")  # per function ("cuda", "gpu", "c", "threads", ...)
def f(x): ...


f(x, _backend="c")  # single call
par.config.backend = "threads"  # process-wide
with par.options(backend="c", num_threads=1):  # scoped block
  f(x)

See Backends and GPUs for Metal, CUDA, and keeping arrays resident on device with par.to_device.

docs.title: Errors and debugging
docs.text:
Anything outside the supported subset fails at compile time with your exact source line:

parakeet.errors.UnsupportedError: numpy.fft.fft is not supported in compiled code
  File "demo.py", line 6, in spectrum
    return np.fft.fft(x)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Run any function uncompiled with f(x, _backend="python") to check whether an issue is in your algorithm or the compiler. To inspect the generated C or GPU kernels, call rms.specialize(x).source (see Errors and debugging).

docs.title: At a glance (NVIDIA L4 & 4-thread CPU)
docs.text:
GPU and CPU cross-framework measurements come from Google Colab VMs with an NVIDIA L4 GPU and a 4-thread CPU (float32, GPU inputs resident on device, explicit synchronization, reference-checked outputs, n = 21 GPU replicates / n = 11 CPU replicates). Download forward-suite raw JSON (0dcb7d5) · Download updated nanoGPT L4 JSON (7bb1dcc).

Baseline policy & Parakeet variants: Every GPU benchmark includes the same general array-compiler matrix (Parakeet, PyTorch eager, torch.compile, JAX jit, and CuPy), plus domain-specific libraries on the tasks they support (Faiss / scikit-learn / SciPy for nearest-neighbor search; PyKeOps for pairwise kernels; edlib / Biopython / Biotite / RDKit for bioinformatics). Where multiple Parakeet spellings, precision modes, or compiler revisions were measured on the same hardware (NumPy vs. par.map, current vs. earlier revision, FP32 vs. TF32, multicore vs. 1-thread), all Parakeet variants are plotted together.

Key takeaways:

  • Exact 1-NN (1,024 × 4,096 × 32):
  • L4 GPU: Parakeet broadcasting NumPy (0.223 ms) and nested par.map (0.225 ms) beat torch.compile(cdist) (0.257 ms), PyTorch cdist (0.251 ms), JAX jit (0.500 ms), PyKeOps (0.953 ms), and CuPy (16.93 ms), trailing only Faiss GpuIndexFlatL2 (0.150 ms).
  • 4-thread CPU: Parakeet (7.91 ms) beats Faiss Flat (8.42 ms), PyKeOps (29.03 ms), SciPy cKDTree (54.27 ms), and NumPy (472.3 ms), just behind scikit-learn brute (6.49 ms).
  • Scaling to 16,384 references (L4 GPU): Tiled pairwise folds cut latency 4.8× (2.597 → 0.542 ms) and global scratch memory 21× (64 → 3 MiB, plus a 16 KiB shared-memory tile per block).
  • Gaussian kernel regression (1,024 × 4,096 × 32):
  • 4-thread CPU: Parakeet (42.99 ms) beats PyKeOps (66.77 ms) and NumPy (505.8 ms, 11.8× faster).
  • L4 GPU: Parakeet (1.053 ms) beats PyKeOps (1.254 ms) and CuPy (17.18 ms), while torch.compile(cdist) (0.308 ms) and JAX jit (0.602 ms) lead.
  • End-to-end nanoGPT training (L4 GPU, zero cuBLAS in Parakeet):
  • Launches/step dropped 63%–66% (214 → 80 on L=2, 437 → 147 on L=4).
  • Small (L=2): 4.57 ms (1.95× faster than PyTorch eager at 8.88 ms).
  • Medium (L=4): 17.81 ms TF32 (beating PyTorch eager at 18.93 ms, within 1.21× of torch.compile at 14.76 ms), with faster compile times (9.35 s / 18.15 s vs. torch.compile 29.3 s and JAX 23.8 s).

docs.title: Methodology notes
docs.text:
• Every benchmark arm is checked against a reference implementation (exact index equality for 1-NN and split finding; tight floating-point tolerance for reductions, attention, and training losses).
  • GPU arms time GPU-resident inputs with explicit CUDA synchronization before and after each replicate; first-call compilation times are recorded separately in the JSON downloads and excluded from warmed medians.
  • On CPU, Parakeet's pairwise fold allocates an 8 KiB (16 × 128 float32) score tile plus 192 B of row summaries per active strip; on GPU, it uses a 16 KiB shared-memory score tile per block and O(Q · #tiles) global partial winners rather than an O(Q · R) distance matrix.

docs.title: Rewrite rules catalog
docs.text:
This reference catalogs the algebraic rewrites Parakeet applies between Python source and native loops, and notes how Parakeet 1.x compares with the two NYU PhD theses behind the original compiler:

  • [R] Alex Rubinsteyn, Runtime Compilation of Array-Oriented Python Programs (NYU, 2014) — type specialization, data-parallel operators, and fusion rules.
  • [H] Eric Hielscher, Locality Optimization for Data Parallel Programs (NYU, 2013; arXiv:1304.1835) — cache/register tiling and loop interchange over operator trees.

(For conceptual motivation and visual walkthroughs, start with Operators & compilation walkthrough and Algebraic laws.)

docs.title: Two rewrite stages
docs.text:
1. During elaboration: array expressions remain delayed (index-to-value functions), so simple producer-consumer chains fuse on construction.
  2. In the middle end: 12 passes in parakeet.transforms.pipeline.PASSES rewrite the emitted operator IR (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, IndexExpand, IndexScatter, IndexWavefront) before loop lowering.

docs.title: Vertical fusion (producer into consumer)
docs.text:
Rule ([R] Fig. 6.1) Python example Implementation notes Map(g, Map(f, X)) → Map(g ∘ f, X) np.tanh(x * a) + b Elaboration + middle end; includes affine coordinate inversion for transpose, shifted-slice, and stencil fusion Map(g, IndexMap(f, σ)) → IndexMap(g ∘ f, σ) par.imap(...) * 2 Elaboration + middle end OuterMap(g, Map(f, X₁), X₂) → fused OuterMap par.allpairs(d, x*s, y) Elaboration Reduce(g, ⊕, Map(f, X)) → Reduce(g ∘ f, ⊕, X) np.sum(x * x) Elaboration + middle end Scatter(⊕, idx, Map(f, X)) → fused IndexScatter np.bincount(idx, weights=w*s) transforms/fusion.py Scan(g, ⊕, ε, Map(f, X)) → fused Scan np.cumsum(x * 2) Elaboration + middle end Map(g, Scan(f, ⊕, ε, X)) → Scan(f, ⊕, g ∘ ε, X) np.cumsum(x) * 2 + 1 Consumer fuses into IndexScan.emit (transforms/fusion.py) Filter(g, p, Map(f, X)) → Filter(g ∘ f, p ∘ f, X) (x * 2)[x * 2 > 0] Predicate and values share fused map Reduce(g, ⊕, Filter(f, p, X)) → FilterReduce np.sum(x[x > 0]) Guarded IndexReduce, zero index allocation (transforms/fusion.py) Filter(q, Filter(p, X)) → Filter(p ∧ q, X) x[x > 0][x[x > 0] < 1] Single short-circuiting compaction (transforms/fusion.py)

Safety guards (extending [R]):

  • Alias safety: every delayed array snapshots the store counter when created; if a potentially aliasing store occurs before consumption, elaboration restarts with that expression materialized eagerly.
  • Duplication guard: [R] has no multi-use guard. Here, an expensive delayed array may be fused at most once; a second consumer or a use inside a loop restarts and evaluates it once.
  • Filter-reduce guards: requires single use of the compacted indices and an explicit identity init (so np.min(x[mask]) still raises ValueError on an empty mask). Inside the fused loop, the gather bounds check is eliminated.

docs.title: Reductions, scans, and linear algebra
docs.text:
• Associativity: reductions parallelize and vectorize only when the combiner is recognizably one of +, *, min, max, and, or, &, |, ^ (however written). Any other user function folds strictly left-to-right.
  • Multi-axis reductions: reduced axes are transposed last (zero-copy view) and folded in one pass per outer coordinate.
  • Parallel scans & filters: associative scans use 3-stage chunk fold → prefix chunk totals → chunk scan; boolean filters use 3-stage count → prefix offsets → parallel scatter.
  • Matrix products & einsum: a @ b lowers to Map((i, j) ↦ Reduce(+, a[i, :] * b[:, j])), so prologues and epilogues fuse directly. Contiguous stride-1 inner loops are ensured by transposing b once when needed (transpose(transpose(x)) → x). Stacked A @ B reshapes to a single tall product. Standalone CPU float A @ B dispatches to NumPy's cblas_?gemm unless config.blas = False.

docs.title: Tiling and locality
docs.text:
[H] thesis concept Parakeet 1.x implementation PermuteReductions (interchange strided inner reduction with stride-1 outer map) Target-aware reduction interchange (transforms/tiling.py): on CPU, hoists strided associative inner reductions (np.sum(X, axis=0)) outside L1-sized output strips; skipped on GPU so warps coalesce across columns TiledMap over nested adverbs Generalized IndexTile + TileStage (transforms/tiling.py, backends/tiled_gpu.py): handles any rank ≥ 2 IndexMap wrapping one IndexReduce (arbitrary folds, Carry states, and prologues/epilogues) → cache + register tiles on CPU, __shared__ / threadgroup tiles on CUDA and Metal Register tiling & unrolling N-D register jamming (lowering.jam_register_tile, 2×4 interior + exact remainder faces on CPU) and 4×4 / 2×2 per-thread register tiles on CUDA/Metal Hardware matrix units Automatic FP32 simdgroup_matrix on Apple Metal; opt-in TF32 nvcuda::wmma on CUDA sm_80+ (config.tensor_cores = True) with double-buffered cp.async TiledReduce / TiledScan L1 column-strip PermuteReductions, invariant row hoisting (normalize), and chunkwise TileScan for affine/bilinear recurrences (general cache-tiled arbitrary TiledScan is not implemented) Online tile-size search Analytical compile-time sizing from TargetProfile (parakeet/target.py) and config.tile_bytes

(Stencils are not maps of reductions over two distinct operands, so they are never tiled—matching [H]'s finding that tiling slows down blur stencils.)

docs.title: Scalars, views, and shape-bucket specialization
docs.text:
Built on the fly during IR construction (leaving CSE, LICM, unrolling, and SIMD vectorization to the system C/CUDA/Metal compiler):

  • Algebraic scalar simplifications: constant folding (NumPy semantics), x + 0, x * 1, x // 1 → x, integer x * 0 → 0 (not floats, preserving -0.0/nan), x ** 2 → x * x, x ** 0.5 → sqrt(x), constant select / boolean short-circuiting.
  • Zero-copy views: slices of slices, transposes, contiguous reshape, and expand_dims reduce purely to offset/stride arithmetic.
  • Redundant check elimination: dimensions already proven equal by a prior broadcast check are not re-checked; loop-bounded indices omit bounds checks.
  • Value & shape-bucket specialization ([R] §6.4 extended):
  • Size-1 dimensions are always static constants (fixing [R]'s 200×1 + 1×300 broadcasting corner case statically).
  • Arguments required at compile time (axis=, keepdims=, tuple lengths) specialize automatically.
  • Tiled/GPU passes propagate finite power-of-2 shape buckets and divisibility (DimInfo(lo, hi, align) via config.shape_specialization), guarding only queried dimensions so aligned sizes (128, 256, 512, 1024, 4096) share one branchless fast-path specialization.

docs.title: Train nanoGPT from scratch
docs.text:
This character-level GPT learns to predict the next character in a short passage. For the fragment para, one training sequence has inputs p a r and targets a r a. At the second position, the model can see p a and must predict r. A causal mask enforces that rule even though the model computes predictions for every position at once.

The six Python blocks below make one complete file. You can copy them in order into train_gpt.py and run python train_gpt.py, or run the same file from the repository. To run the repository version, use Python 3.11 or newer and a C compiler.

git clone https://github.com/iskandr/parakeet.git
cd parakeet
python -m pip install -e .
python -m examples.nanogpt

The text is embedded in the script. The default run trains on batches of 16 sequences, each 32 characters long, for 60 steps.

docs.title: Normalize one position at a time
docs.text:
One input sequence becomes a matrix of shape (context, width). Each row holds one character's embedding. LayerNorm is a plain @dataclass with a __call__ method that normalizes across the features of each row. Parakeet lowers @dataclass modules and their pure methods directly during compilation with no PyObject overhead. Later, each row passed to softmax holds attention scores from one position to every position in the sequence; subtracting the row maximum keeps the exponential stable.

"""A character-level GPT trained with parakeet.value_and_grad.

The model is a small hierarchy of ``@dataclass`` modules (``LayerNorm``,
``Block``, ``NanoGPT``) holding plain NumPy arrays. ``par.value_and_grad``
differentiates the batch loss with respect to the entire model dataclass, and
Adam updates each parameter array in plain Python.
"""

import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, fields, is_dataclass

import numpy as np

import parakeet as par

N_HEAD = 2


def softmax(x):
  e = np.exp(x - np.max(x, axis=1, keepdims=True))
  return e / np.sum(e, axis=1, keepdims=True)


@dataclass
class LayerNorm:
  gain: np.ndarray
  bias: np.ndarray

  def __call__(self, x):
    mu = np.mean(x, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    var = np.mean((x - mu) ** 2, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + 1e-5) * self.gain + self.bias

docs.title: Mix information across visible characters
docs.text:
Block groups one transformer layer's norms, attention projections (wq, wk, wv, wo), and feed-forward weights (w1, b1, w2, b2). Each attention head uses part of the model width, computes a (context, context) score matrix, masks future positions before softmax, and projects back through wo. The block adds the attention output to its input, runs a two-layer tanh MLP on each position, and adds that residual too.

@dataclass
class Block:
  ln1: LayerNorm
  wq: np.ndarray
  wk: np.ndarray
  wv: np.ndarray
  wo: np.ndarray
  ln2: LayerNorm
  w1: np.ndarray
  b1: np.ndarray
  w2: np.ndarray
  b2: np.ndarray

  def attention(self, x, causal):
    """Causal self-attention over one sequence: x is (T, C)."""
    head_width = x.shape[1] // N_HEAD
    q, k, v = x @ self.wq, x @ self.wk, x @ self.wv
    out = np.zeros_like(x)
    for h in range(N_HEAD):
      lo, hi = h * head_width, (h + 1) * head_width
      scores = q[:, lo:hi] @ k[:, lo:hi].T / np.sqrt(head_width)
      weights = softmax(np.where(causal, scores, -1e9))
      out = out + (weights @ v[:, lo:hi]) @ self.wo[lo:hi]
    return out

  def __call__(self, x, causal):
    x = x + self.attention(self.ln1(x), causal)
    h = np.tanh(self.ln2(x) @ self.w1 + self.b1)
    return x + h @ self.w2 + self.b2

docs.title: Score one sequence, then a batch
docs.text:
NanoGPT.sequence_loss embeds the token IDs (self.wte[tokens] + self.wpe), runs each block in self.blocks, projects to vocabulary logits with self.ln_f(x) @ self.head, and computes the mean negative log-probability of the next character at each position.

In loss, both tokens and targets have shape (batch, context). par.map applies model.sequence_loss across every (inp, tgt) pair in the batch, and np.mean averages the per-sequence losses. par.value_and_grad(loss) compiles one native function returning both the scalar loss and a NanoGPT dataclass holding the gradient of every parameter array.

@dataclass
class NanoGPT:
  wte: np.ndarray
  wpe: np.ndarray
  blocks: tuple
  ln_f: LayerNorm
  head: np.ndarray

  def sequence_loss(self, tokens, targets, causal):
    x = self.wte[tokens] + self.wpe
    for blk in self.blocks:
      x = blk(x, causal)
    logits = self.ln_f(x) @ self.head
    z = logits - np.max(logits, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    logp = z - np.log(np.sum(np.exp(z), axis=1, keepdims=True))
    return -np.mean(logp[np.arange(len(targets)), targets])


def loss(model, tokens, targets, causal):
  per_sequence = par.map(lambda inp, tgt: model.sequence_loss(inp, tgt, causal), tokens, targets)
  return np.mean(per_sequence)


loss_and_grad = par.value_and_grad(loss)

docs.title: Build the model
docs.text:
init constructs a NanoGPT instance containing the token and position embedding tables, a tuple of Block modules, the final LayerNorm, and the output projection head. With the defaults, wte has shape (vocab, 32) and head has shape (32, vocab).

def init(vocab, context, width, layers, rng):
  def w(*shape):
    return rng.normal(0.0, 0.02, shape)

  def norm():
    return LayerNorm(np.ones(width), np.zeros(width))

  def one_block():
    return Block(
      ln1=norm(),
      wq=w(width, width),
      wk=w(width, width),
      wv=w(width, width),
      wo=w(width, width),
      ln2=norm(),
      w1=w(width, 4 * width),
      b1=np.zeros(4 * width),
      w2=w(4 * width, width),
      b2=np.zeros(width),
    )

  return NanoGPT(
    wte=w(vocab, width),
    wpe=w(context, width),
    blocks=tuple(one_block() for _ in range(layers)),
    ln_f=norm(),
    head=w(width, vocab),
  )

docs.title: Update every parameter with Adam
docs.text:
loss_and_grad returns the batch loss and a NanoGPT gradient tree matching the structure of model. tree_map walks matching tuples and dataclass fields together so Adam can update embeddings, norms, biases, and projections with the same few lines. m tracks the moving average of gradients and v tracks the moving average of squared gradients.

def tree_map(f, *trees):
  first = trees[0]
  if isinstance(first, tuple):
    return tuple(tree_map(f, *parts) for parts in zip(*trees))
  if is_dataclass(first):
    return type(first)(*(tree_map(f, *(getattr(t, fl.name) for t in trees)) for fl in fields(first)))
  return f(*trees)


def adam(model, grads, m, v, step, lr=3e-3, b1=0.9, b2=0.99):
  m = tree_map(lambda m, g: b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g, m, grads)
  v = tree_map(lambda v, g: b2 * v + (1 - b2) * g * g, v, grads)
  scale = lr * np.sqrt(1 - b2**step) / (1 - b1**step)
  model = tree_map(lambda p, m, v: p - scale * m / (np.sqrt(v) + 1e-8), model, m, v)
  return model, m, v


def train_step(model, m, v, step, tokens, targets, causal):
  value, grads = loss_and_grad(model, tokens, targets, causal)
  model, m, v = adam(model, grads, m, v, step)
  return value, model, m, v

docs.title: Train on shifted character windows
docs.text:
main assigns one integer ID to each distinct character in TEXT. For a sample starting at offset i, tokens starts at i and targets starts at i + 1. Stacking those windows gives the two arrays consumed by par.map. The lower triangle of causal includes the diagonal, so each position can read its own input when predicting the following character.

TEXT = (
  "parakeet compiles numerical python. it fuses array expressions into loops, "
  "runs them on every core, and now differentiates them too. "
) * 8


def main(steps=60, batch=16, context=32, width=32, layers=2, seed=0, verbose=False):
  rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
  chars = sorted(set(TEXT))
  data = np.array([chars.index(c) for c in TEXT])
  model = init(len(chars), context, width, layers, rng)
  m = tree_map(np.zeros_like, model)
  v = tree_map(np.zeros_like, model)
  causal = np.tril(np.ones((context, context))) > 0
  first = last = None
  start = time.perf_counter()
  for step in range(1, steps + 1):
    at = rng.integers(0, len(data) - context - 1, batch)
    tokens = np.stack([data[i : i + context] for i in at])
    targets = np.stack([data[i + 1 : i + context + 1] for i in at])
    value, model, m, v = train_step(model, m, v, step, tokens, targets, causal)
    first = value if first is None else first
    last = value
    if verbose and (step == 1 or step % 20 == 0):
      print(f"step {step:3d}  loss {value:.3f}  ({time.perf_counter() - start:.1f}s)")
  assert last < 0.8 * first, (first, last)
  return first, last


if __name__ == "__main__":
  main(verbose=True)

The first training step compiles the forward and gradient kernels; subsequent steps reuse the compiled native code. With --verbose (the default when run as a script), main prints the cross-entropy loss at steps 1, 20, 40, and 60 and asserts that training makes progress (final loss below 80% of step 1). Using the fixed seed=0 above, the printed loss drops from 3.173 at step 1 to 2.307 (step 20), 1.796 (step 40), and 1.250 (step 60) on GPU (with nearly identical values on CPU).

For larger four-head training runs where the Adam update is also compiled into the training step, see the nanoGPT training benchmark. The compact two-head walkthrough above keeps Adam in plain Python so every line is easy to follow.
